Qíbó answered:
"The *jùyáng* (巨陽, Greater Yang)
is the category to which all Yang meridians belong.
Its vessel connects to the Wind Mansion (Fēngfǔ) point,
therefore it is the chief controller of Qi for all Yang meridians.
When a person is injured by cold,
it results in febrile disease.
Even if the fever is severe, they will not die.
However, those who are affected by cold in both ways
will inevitably die."
31.2 The Emperor (Dì) said:
"I wish to hear about its characteristics."
Qíbó said:
"On the first day of *shānghán* (傷寒),
the *jùyáng* (巨陽) receives it,
therefore there is headache, neck pain, and stiffness of the lower back and spine.
On the second day, the Yángmíng receives it.
The Yángmíng governs the flesh.

Therefore, there is body heat, eye pain, and a dry nose,
making it impossible to lie down.
On the third day,
the Shǎoyáng receives it.
The Shǎoyáng governs the gallbladder.

On the fifth day,

On the sixth day,

The Juéyīn meridian follows the genitals and connects to the liver.

The three Yīn and three Yáng,
the five Zàng organs and six Fǔ organs,
If they all receive the disease,

if it has been three days,

All relapses

Observe its deficiency or excess,

If it can be treated, it must be treated.

The Emperor asked:

Qíbó said:
The Yángmíng channel

Its blood and qi are abundant,

After three days, its qi is exhausted,

In general, illnesses that become wēn (febrile disease) from shānghán (cold damage)
are called bìngwēn (febrile disease) if they occur before the summer solstice.
Those that occur after the summer solstice are called bìngshǔ (summerheat disease).
With summerheat, sweat should be allowed to flow freely,

*Píng Rè Bìng Lùn Piān* (Treatise on Assessing Febrile Diseases), Chapter Thirty-three
33.1 The Yellow Emperor asked,

Therefore, first suffering from evil,
Shǎo Yīn 少陰 and its exterior-interior relationship,

Unable to lie straight on the back;

Chapter 34: Discussion on Counter Regulation
34.1.1 The Yellow Emperor asked:

therefore, the body feels cold as if emerging from water.

Dú zhì zhě bùnéng shēngzhǎng yě,

34.3 The Emperor said:

Good.
Chapter 35: On Malaria
35.1 The Yellow Emperor asked:
"Malaria is always caused by wind.
Why does its onset and recurrence occur at specific times?"
What is the reason for this?
Qíbó replied:
"At the onset of malaria,
it first begins in the fine hairs of the skin.
Stretching and yawning then occur.
There is shivering and chattering of the jaws.
The lower back and spine both ache.
When the cold subsides, both the interior and exterior become hot.
The headache is as if the head is splitting.
There is thirst and a desire for cold drinks."
The Emperor said:
"What qi causes this?
I wish to hear the reason."
Qíbó said:
"It is the alternating conflict between yin and yang above and below,
deficiency and repletion alternating.
It is the mutual displacement of yin and yang.
When yang combines with yin,
then yin becomes replete and yang becomes deficient.
When the Yángmíng channel is deficient,
then there is shivering and chattering of the jaws.
When the Jùyáng 巨陽 (Bladder meridian) is deficient,
there will be pain in the lower back, upper back, head, and nape of the neck.
When all three Yáng 三陽 are deficient,
then the Yīn 陰 energy prevails.
When the Yīn 陰 energy prevails,
then the bones become cold and painful.
When cold arises from within,
therefore both the interior and exterior are cold.
When Yáng 陽 is abundant, then there is external heat.
When Yīn 陰 is deficient, then there is internal heat.
When both the exterior and interior are hot,
then there is panting and thirst.
Therefore, there is a desire for cold drinks.
All this is obtained from being harmed by summer heat.
When the heat energy is abundant,
it is stored within the skin,
outside the intestines and stomach.
This is where the yíng qì 榮氣 resides.
This causes people to have loose and sparse sweat pores,
the pores open,
and they then contract autumn qi.
Sweating and encountering wind,
and obtaining it from bathing,
water qi lodges within the skin,
residing together with the wèiqì 衛氣.
The wèiqì 衛氣,
during the day circulates in the Yáng 陽,
and at night circulates in the Yīn 陰.
This *qì* receives *yáng* and goes outward,
receives *yīn* and presses inward,
the inward and outward press against each other,
and therefore it occurs daily.
35.2 The Emperor said:
What causes it to occur on alternate days?
Qíbó said:
The lodging place of its *qì* is deep,
pressing inward towards *yīn*,
*yáng qì* alone arises,
*yīn* evil adheres internally,
*yīn* and *yáng* contend but cannot exit,
and therefore it occurs on alternate days.
The Emperor said:
Good. What *qì* causes it to occur late in the day or early in the day?
What *qì* causes it to be so?
Qíbó said:
The evil *qì* lodges in the Fēngfǔ (Wind Mansion),
following the spine downwards.
The defensive *qì* gathers at the Fēngfǔ once every day and night.
The next day, it descends one joint each day.
Therefore, its onset is late.
This is because it first lodges in the back.
Every time it reaches the Fēngfǔ, the pores open.
When the pores open, the evil *qì* enters.
When the evil *qì* enters, the disease occurs.
Therefore, the daily onset becomes increasingly late.
It originates from the Fēngfǔ (風府) point.
[It] descends one section each day.
In twenty-five days, it descends to the sacrum.
On the twenty-sixth day, it enters the spine.
Its qi ascends.
In nine days, it emerges from the center of the quēpén (缺盆).
Its qi becomes higher each day.
Therefore, the onset occurs earlier each day.
Those with intermittent daily attacks
are due to pathogenic qi pressing internally on the five zàng (五藏) organs,
transversely connecting to the mùyuán (募原) area.
Its pathway is long.
Its qi is deep.
Its movement is slow.
It cannot travel together with the wèiqì (衛氣).
It cannot all emerge.
Therefore, it occurs intermittently daily.
35.3 The Emperor said:
You say that when the wèiqì (衛氣) arrives at the Fēngfǔ (風府) point,
the interstices of the skin open,
and when they open, pathogenic qi enters,

Now, the wèiqì (衛氣) descends one section each day.

Qíbó (歧伯) said:
This is when evil qi lodges in the head and nape of the neck, following the spine downward.
Therefore, deficiency and excess are different,
and the site of affliction by evil varies.
Thus, it may not necessarily correspond to the Fēngfǔ (風府) point.
Therefore, if evil affects the head and nape of the neck,
qi arrives at the head and nape of the neck, and illness arises.
If it affects the back,
qi arrives at the back, and illness arises.
If it affects the waist and spine,
qi arrives at the waist and spine, and illness arises.
If it affects the hands and feet,
qi arrives at the hands and feet, and illness arises.
Wherever the wèiqì (衛氣) is located,
when it combines with evil qi,
then illness arises.
Therefore, wind has no fixed residence.
Wherever the wèiqì (衛氣) emerges,
it necessarily opens the pores.
Wherever evil qi combines,
that is its residence.
The Emperor said,
"Good."
35.4 As for wind and malaria,
they are similar and of the same category.
Yet wind is constantly present,
while malaria has times of remission. Why is this?
Qíbó (歧伯) said,
The pathogenic influences (fēng qì) remain in their location,
therefore they are constantly present.
Malarial influences penetrate along the meridians (jīngluò) and settle within, approaching thinly;
therefore the protective qi (wèi qì) responds and arises.
The Emperor (Dì) said:
Malaria that manifests first with cold and then with heat,
what is the reason for this?
Qíbó said:
Having been harmed by the great heat (dàshǔ) of summer,
one's sweat flows profusely,
the pores (còulǐ) are opened,
then encountering the chilly and cold (qīcāng zhī shuǐ hán) water of summer,
it is stored within the pores and skin.
Then, having been harmed by wind in autumn,
the disease is formed.
Now, cold is
a yin qi (yīn qì);
wind is
a yang qi (yáng qì).
First harmed by cold,
and then harmed by wind,
therefore, it is first cold and then heat.
The disease arises according to the seasons;
it is named cold malaria (hán nüè).
The Emperor (Dì) said:
That which is first heat and then cold,
what is the reason for this?
Qíbó said:
This is first injured by wind and then injured by cold;
therefore, it is first hot and then cold.
It also occurs at specific times.
It is called wēn nüè (溫瘧, warm malaria).
As for those that are only hot and not cold,
the Yin Qi is exhausted first,
and the Yang Qi is released alone,
which then causes shortness of breath, vexation, and restlessness.
The hands and feet are hot, and there is a desire to vomit.
This is called dàn nüè (癉瘧, jaundice malaria).
35.5 The Dì (帝, Yellow Emperor) said:
The classic says to drain what is excessive
and to supplement what is insufficient.
Now heat is excessive,
and cold is insufficient.
The coldness of malaria
cannot be warmed by hot soup or fire,
and when it is hot,
ice water cannot cool it.
These are all examples of excess and deficiency.
At this time,
a good doctor cannot stop it.
It must be allowed to weaken on its own
before it is punctured.
What is the reason for this?
I wish to hear the explanation.
Qíbó (歧伯) said:
The *Jīng* says: Do not needle when there is a *xiāo xiāo*
do not needle when there is a *hún hún* pulse,
do not needle when there is *lù lù* sweating.
Therefore, if these conditions are present, the disease is considered to be in reverse and cannot be treated.
Now, at the onset of malaria,
the *yáng qì* converges on the *yīn*.
At this time,
the *yáng* is deficient and the *yīn* is abundant,
and there is no *qì* on the exterior,
therefore, there is first cold and shivering.
When the *yīn qì* reverses to its extreme,
then it returns to the *yáng*.
When the *yáng* and *yīn* again converge on the exterior,
then the *yīn* is deficient and the *yáng* is replete,
therefore, there is first heat and thirst.
Now, the malarial *qì*,
if it converges on the *yáng*, then the *yáng* prevails;
if it converges on the *yīn*, then the *yīn* prevails.
When the *yīn* prevails, there is cold;
when the *yáng* prevails, there is heat.
Malaria
is caused by the *qì* of wind and cold being inconsistent.
When the disease reaches its extreme, it reverses.
When the disease manifests,
it is like the heat of fire,
like wind and rain that cannot be withstood.
Therefore, the *Jīng* says:
"When something is at its peak, it will surely decline;
Because of its decline,
the matter will surely greatly flourish.
This is what it means.
When malaria has not yet developed,
the Yin has not yet combined with the Yang,
the Yang has not yet combined with the Yin,
therefore regulate it,
the True Qi obtains peace,
the Evil Qi then disappears,
therefore skilled doctors cannot treat what has already developed,
because its Qi is rebellious.
The Emperor said:
Good. How to attack it,
what about early or late?
Qí Bó said:
When malaria is about to develop,
when the Yin and Yang are about to shift,
it must begin from the four extremities,
the Yang has already been injured,
the Yin follows it,
therefore, beforehand, firmly bind that location,
so that Evil Qi cannot enter,
and Yin Qi cannot exit,
carefully observe and see where it is in the superficial collaterals, where they are full, hard, and bloody, all of that should be taken.
This is where the True (Qi) has gone but has not yet been able to combine.
The Emperor said:
If malaria does not develop,
what should be the response?
Qí Bó said:
"Malaria,
must have periods of increased severity and periods of remission.
It occurs where the pathogenic qi is located.
If the disease is in the *yáng*,
then there will be heat and a rapid pulse;
if it is in the *yīn*,
then there will be cold and a slow pulse.
When it reaches its extreme, both *yīn* and *yáng* decline,
and the *wèi qì* separates,
therefore the disease subsides.
When the *wèi qì* gathers,
then the disease recurs."
35.6. The Emperor said:
"Sometimes there is an interval of two days or even several days before it occurs,
sometimes there is thirst, sometimes not.
What is the reason for this?"
Qí Bó said:
"The interval days occur because
the pathogenic qi and the *wèi qì* are lodged in the six *fǔ* organs,
and sometimes they become misaligned,
unable to coordinate with each other.
Therefore, it subsides for several days before recurring.
Malaria is
the alternating dominance of *yīn* and *yáng*.
It is sometimes severe and sometimes not,
therefore there is sometimes thirst and sometimes not."
The Emperor said:
"It is said that injury from summer heat
inevitably leads to malaria in autumn.
Why is it that malaria does not always appear then?"
Qí Bó said:
"This corresponds to the four seasons.
Diseases with different manifestations
are contrary to the four seasons.
Those who become ill in autumn experience severe cold.
Those who become ill in winter experience less severe cold.
Those who become ill in spring dislike wind.
Those who become ill in summer sweat profusely."
35.7 The Emperor said:
"Both warm malaria and cold malaria, where do they reside,
in which organ do they dwell?"
Qí Bó said:
"Warm malaria
is contracted in winter by exposure to wind.
Cold qi is stored within the bone marrow.
When spring arrives, the yang qi greatly flourishes,
and the pathogenic qi cannot escape on its own.
Then, encountering great heat,
the brain marrow melts,
the muscles waste away,
the skin pores open and drain,
or there is some exertion of force,
and the pathogenic qi and sweat all exit.
This illness is stored in the kidney;
its *qì* first emerges from within and goes to the exterior.
In such cases,
the *yīn* is deficient and the *yáng* is excessive.
When the *yáng* is excessive, it becomes hot.
When it declines, the *qì* reverts and re-enters.
When it enters, the *yáng* is deficient.
When the *yáng* is deficient, it becomes cold.
Therefore, it is first hot and then cold,
and is called *wēn nüè* (warm malaria).
The Emperor asked:
What about *dàn nüè* (lingering malaria)?
Qíbó said:
*Dàn nüè* is when
the *fèi* (lung) inherently has hot *qì*, which is abundant in the body.
A counterflow rises upward.
The *zhōng qì* (central *qì*) is substantial and does not vent outward.
Due to some exertion,
the *còu lǐ* (cutaneous pores) open.
*Fēng hán* (wind-cold) lodges within the skin
and between the muscles, causing it to manifest.
When it manifests, the *yáng qì* is abundant.
If the *yáng qì* is abundant and does not decline,
then illness occurs.
Its *qì* does not reach the *yīn*.
Therefore, there is only heat and no cold.
The *qì* is internally stored in the *xīn* (heart)
and externally lodges between the muscles,
It causes people to waste away and lose flesh,
therefore it is called dàn疟 (dànnüè), "consumption malaria."
The Emperor said,
"Good."
Chapter 36: "Treating Malaria by Puncture"
36.1 Malaria of the Foot Taiyang channel
causes lower back pain, heaviness of the head,
and cold starting from the back.
First cold, then heat,
with a sensation of being scorched and parched.
When the heat stops, sweat comes out,
and it is difficult to cure.
Puncture the xiè (郄) point in the middle and bleed it.
Malaria of the Foot Shaoyang channel
causes the body to feel loose and weak,
the cold is not severe,
the heat is not severe,
and there is a dislike of seeing people.
Upon seeing people, the heart trembles.
The heat is greater and the sweating is profuse.
Puncture the Foot Shaoyang channel.
Malaria of the Foot Yangming channel
causes one to first feel cold and shivering for a long time before becoming hot.
When the heat subsides, sweat comes out, and one likes to see sunlight, moonlight, and firelight,
and then feels comfortable.
Puncture the Foot Yangming channel on the dorsum of the foot.
Malaria of the Foot Taiyin channel
Causes unhappiness,
likes to sigh deeply,
has no appetite,
often experiences chills and fever with sweating,
when the illness arrives, one vomits easily,
and is weakened after vomiting,
then take it.
Malaria of the Foot Shaoyin
causes severe vomiting,
frequent chills and fever,
with more fever and less chills;
wanting to close doors and windows to stay inside,
the illness is difficult to cure.
Malaria of the Foot Jueyin
causes lower back pain, fullness in the lower abdomen,
and difficulty urinating,
resembling strangury,
but it is not strangury,
frequent urination,
with a sense of fear and insufficient Qi,
and a feeling of unease in the abdomen;
puncture the Foot Jueyin.
36.2 Concerning Lung Malaria,
it causes the person to feel cold in the heart,
extreme cold followed by fever,
and between fevers, the person is easily startled,
as if seeing something;
Needle the Hand Taiyin and Yangming.
For malaria of the heart,
it causes vexation and a great desire for cold water, but with much aversion to cold and
not much heat,
needle the Hand Shaoyin.
For malaria of the liver,
it causes the complexion to be pale and one to sigh deeply,
with a state resembling death,
needle the Foot Jueyin to draw blood.
For malaria of the spleen,
it causes cold,
abdominal pain,
and when heat occurs, rumbling in the intestines,
and after rumbling, sweating,
needle the Foot Taiyin.
For malaria of the kidneys,
it causes shivering,
pain in the loins and spine with difficult bowel movements,
blurred vision,
and cold hands and feet,
needle the Foot Taiyang and Shaoyin.
For malaria of the stomach,
it causes one to be on the verge of illness,
to be easily hungry but unable to eat,
and to have fullness in the limbs and a large abdomen after eating,
needle the transverse vessels of the Foot Yangming and Taiyin to draw blood.
36.3.1 When malaria is developing and the body is just becoming hot,
Puncture the dòngmài (動脈) on the dorsum of the foot
, open its cavity and let out the blood
, immediately relieving the chills.
For malaria about to cause chills, puncture the shǒu yángmíng (手陽明), tàiyīn (太陰), zú yángmíng (足陽明), and tàiyīn (太陰) channels.
36.3.2 If the malaria pulse is full and large
, quickly puncture the back shù (俞) points
, using a medium-sized needle, one point each beside the wǔ qūyú (胠俞) points
, adapting to the patient's body type (fat or thin) and letting out blood.
If the malaria pulse is small and solid
, quickly moxa the shǎo yīn (少陰) on the tibia
and puncture the jǐng (井) points of the fingers.
If the malaria pulse is full and large
, quickly puncture the back shù (俞) points
, one wǔ qūyú (胠俞) and one back shù (俞) point each
, adapting to guide the needle to the blood.
If the malaria pulse is slow, large, and deficient
, it is better to use medicine
, not suitable to use acupuncture.
In general, for treating malaria, treat it before it fully manifests
, such as shortly before the attack, then you can treat it
, if you miss this timing, then you'll miss the opportunity.
For all types of malaria where the pulse is not visible
, puncture and bleed the spaces between the ten fingers
, the bleeding will certainly alleviate it
, first look for red spots on the body resembling small beans and remove them all.
36.3.3 The twelve types of malaria
Their onsets occur at different times.
Observe the form of the illness
in order to know which meridian's illness it is.
First, when it begins, like within the space of a meal, then puncture it.
One puncture will cause it to wane;
two punctures will make it understood;
three punctures will cause it to cease.
If it doesn't cease,
puncture the two vessels below the tongue to bleed them.
If it still doesn't cease,
puncture the abundant meridian in the *xì* point to bleed it.
Furthermore, puncturing those below the nape on either side of the spine will surely cause it to cease.
The two vessels below the tongue
are the Liánquán 廉泉 points.
36.3.4 When puncturing for malaria,
one must first ask where the illness first manifests;
puncture that place first.
For those who first experience headache or heaviness,
first puncture the head and between both foreheads and both eyebrows to bleed them.
For those who first experience pain in the nape and back,
puncture that place first.
For those who first experience pain in the waist and spine,
first puncture the *xì* point to bleed it.
For those who first experience pain in the arms and hands,
first puncture between the ten fingers of the Hand *Shàoyīn* and *Yángmíng* meridians.
For those who first experience soreness and pain in the feet and shins,
first puncture between the ten fingers of the Foot *Yángmíng* meridian to bleed them.
Wind malaria.
When the malaria manifests, there is sweating and aversion to wind.
Puncture the blood vessels of the Bèi Shū (背俞) points of the Three Yang meridians.
If the bones (䯒) are sore and painful, and pressing on them is indescribable, it is called Fú Suí (胕髓) disease.
Use a chisel needle to puncture Jué Gǔ (絕骨) and let out blood.
It will be immediately cured.
For minor aches and pains in the body,
puncture Zhì Yīn (至陰).
If there is no bleeding from the Jǐng (井) points of the various Yin meridians,
puncture once every other day.
For malaria without thirst,
which occurs every other day,
puncture the Foot Taiyang meridian.
For malaria with thirst, which occurs every other day,
puncture the Foot Shaoyang meridian.
For febrile malaria without sweating,
use the Fifty-Nine Punctures.
Treatise on Qi Reversal, chapter thirty-seven.
37.1 The Yellow Emperor asked:
What causes the shifting of cold and heat in the five Zàng (藏) organs and six Fǔ (府) organs?
Qí Bó (歧伯) said:
If the kidneys transfer cold to the liver,
there will be carbuncles, swelling, and shortness of breath.
If the spleen transfers cold to the liver,
there will be carbuncles, swelling, and muscle spasms.
If the liver transfers cold to the heart,
Madness is internal.
If the heart transfers cold to the lungs,
the lungs waste away.
If the lungs waste away, the patient drinks one [unit] and urinates two [units],
and death is incurable.
If the lungs transfer cold to the kidneys,
it becomes surging water.
Surging water is [characterized by]:
pressing on the abdomen reveals it is not firm,
and water qi resides in the large intestine.
When walking quickly, it gurgles like a sack filled with liquid;
it is a disease of water.
37.2 If the spleen transfers heat to the liver,
it becomes fright and nosebleed.
If the liver transfers heat to the heart,
then death results.
If the heart transfers heat to the lungs,
it is transmitted as wasting of the diaphragm.
If the lungs transfer heat to the kidneys,
it is transmitted as mild tetanus.
If the kidneys transfer heat to the spleen,
it is transmitted as deficiency,
intestinal bloody flux results in death,
and it is incurable.
37.3 If the uterus transfers heat to the bladder,
it results in strangury and bloody urine.
When the bladder transfers heat to the small intestine,
there is difficulty with the diaphragm and intestines,
resulting in *kǒu mí* (oral thrush) above.
When the small intestine transfers heat to the large intestine,
it causes *fú jiǎ* (abdominal masses) and sinking sensations.
When the large intestine transfers heat to the stomach,
the person eats well but becomes thin; this is called *shí yì*.
When the stomach transfers heat to the gall bladder,
this is also called *shí yì*.
When the gall bladder transfers heat to the brain,
then there is a pungent smell in the nose, and *bí yuān* (nasal congestion).
*Bí yuān*
is the incessant dripping of turbid nasal discharge.
It can progress to bleeding, blurred vision, and closed eyes;
therefore, it is acquired by *qì jué* (qi collapse).
Chapter Thirty-Eight: On Coughing.
38.1 The Yellow Emperor asked:
What causes the lungs to induce coughing?
Qí Bó replied:
All the five viscera and six bowels
can induce coughing,
it is not only the lungs.
The Emperor said:
I wish to hear their conditions.
Qí Bó said:
The skin and hair
The lung's corresponding exterior
is the skin and hair, which are the first to receive pathogenic influences;
pathogenic influences follow this relationship.
If cold food and drink enter the stomach,
they ascend from the lung vessel to the lung;
then the lung becomes cold.
When the lung is cold, the exterior and interior combine,
and pathogenic influences take advantage of this and lodge there,
resulting in lung cough (fèi ké).
Each of the five viscera receives disease according to its season;
if it is not its season,
each transmits the disease to the others.
Humans correspond to Heaven and Earth;
therefore, each of the five viscera governs
and is susceptible to cold at its proper time,
and then receives disease.
If mild, it manifests as cough;
if severe, it manifests as diarrhea or pain.
In autumn, the lung is the first to receive pathogenic influences;
in spring, the liver is the first to receive them;
in summer, the heart is the first to receive them;
during the extreme Yin season, the spleen is the first to receive them;
in winter, the kidney is the first to receive them.
38.2.1 The Dì (Emperor) said:
How are they differentiated?
Qí Bó said:
The characteristics of lung cough (fèi ké) are
Coughing and panting with sounds,
in severe cases, spitting blood.
The symptoms of heart cough:
Coughing causes heart pain.
A feeling of obstruction in the throat,
in severe cases, swelling of the throat and throat paralysis.
The symptoms of liver cough:
Coughing causes pain under both ribs,
in severe cases, unable to turn the body;
turning causes fullness under both armpits.
The symptoms of spleen cough:
Coughing causes pain under the right rib, a dull pain extending to the shoulder and back,
in severe cases, unable to move;
movement intensifies the cough.
The symptoms of kidney cough:
Coughing causes pulling pain in the waist and back,
in severe cases, coughing up saliva.
38.2.2 The Dì said:
What about the coughs of the Six Fǔ organs?
Where does the disease originate?
Qí Bó said:
Prolonged coughs of the Five Zàng organs
will then spread to the Six Fǔ organs.
If spleen cough does not cease,
then the stomach receives it.
The symptoms of stomach cough:
Coughing and vomiting;
Severe vomiting can cause the expulsion of roundworms.
If liver cough (gān ké) persists,
then the gallbladder (dǎn) is affected.
The manifestation of gallbladder cough
is coughing and vomiting of bile.
If lung cough (fèi ké) persists,
then the large intestine (dàcháng) is affected.
The manifestation of large intestine cough
is coughing and incontinence.
If heart cough (xīn ké) persists,
then the small intestine (xiǎocháng) is affected.
The manifestation of small intestine cough
is coughing and loss of gas;
both gas and cough are lost together.
If kidney cough (shèn ké) persists,
then the bladder (pángguāng) is affected.
The manifestation of bladder cough
is coughing and incontinence of urine.
If a cough persists for a long time,
then the Sanjiao (sānjiāo) is affected.
The manifestation of Sanjiao cough
is coughing with abdominal distension,
lack of desire to eat or drink.
All of these gather in the stomach (wèi)
and are related to the lungs (fèi),
causing a person to have excessive nasal discharge and saliva, facial swelling, and qi rebellion.
The Emperor (Dì) asked:
How should it be treated?
Qíbó said:
To treat the Zàng organs,
treat their Shū points;
to treat the Fǔ organs,
treat their Hé points.
For edema,
treat their meridians.
The Emperor said:
Good.
Discussion on Alleviating Pain, Section Thirty-Nine
39.1 The Yellow Emperor asked, saying:
"I have heard that those who speak well about Heaven
must have validation in people;
those who speak well about antiquity
must have conformity with the present;
those who speak well about people
must have verification in themselves.
If it is like this,
then the Dao is not confused, and the essential numbers are exhausted.
This is what is called understanding.
Now I ask you, Master,
to make your words understandable,
visible when looked at,
obtainable when felt,
and verifiable in oneself to dispel ignorance and resolve doubts.
May I have the opportunity to hear this?"
Qí Bó bowed again, kowtowed, and replied:
"What kind of question is this?"
39.2.1 The Emperor said:
"I wish to hear about the sudden pain in people's five viscera,
what kind of Qi causes it?"
Qí Bó replied:
"The meridians circulate without ceasing,
revolving continuously,
if cold Qi enters the meridians and stagnates,
weeping and not flowing,
lodging outside the vessels, blood will be deficient;
lodging within the vessels, Qi will not flow,
hence the sudden onset of pain."
39.2.2 The Emperor said:
"The pain either stops suddenly,
or the pain is severe and unremitting,
or the pain is so severe that it cannot be pressed,
or pressing it stops the pain,
or pressing it is of no benefit,
or the breathing moves in response to the hand,
or the heart and back pull against each other in pain,
or the hypochondria and lower abdomen pull against each other in pain,
or the abdominal pain extends to the genitals and inner thighs,
or the pain lingers overnight and forms an accumulation,
or there is a sudden death from pain, unaware of one's surroundings,
only to revive after a short while,
Some experience pain accompanied by vomiting,
some have abdominal pain followed by diarrhea,
some have pain accompanied by constipation.
All these pains
manifest in different forms.
How can they be distinguished?
39.2.3 Qíbó said:
When cold qi lodges outside the vessels,
the vessels become cold.
When the vessels are cold, they contract and curl up.
When they contract and curl up, the vessels become constricted and tense.
Constriction and tenseness then outwardly pull on the small collaterals,
hence the sudden onset of pain.
When warmth is applied, the pain stops immediately.
But if repeatedly exposed to cold,
the pain will persist for a long time.
When cold qi lodges within the meridians,
and clashes with warm qi,
the vessels become full.
When full, there is pain that cannot be touched.
If cold qi lingers,
and warm qi rises from above,
the vessels become distended and the blood and qi are disordered.
Therefore, the pain is severe and cannot be touched.
When cold qi lodges between the intestines and stomach,
below the membrane,
the blood cannot disperse,
When the small luò (小絡) vessels contract sharply, pain ensues.
Pressing on them disperses the blood and qì (氣).
Therefore, pressing stops the pain.
When cold qì (寒氣) lodges in the xiá jí (俠脊) vessels,
deep pressure cannot reach it.
Therefore, pressing is of no benefit.
When cold qì (寒氣) lodges in the chōng (衝) vessel,
the chōng (衝) vessel originates at Guānyuán (關元),
and ascends straight up the abdomen.
If cold qì (寒氣) lodges there, the vessel does not flow.
If the vessel does not flow, qì (氣) is obstructed because of it.
Therefore, panting and movement respond to the hand.
When cold qì (寒氣) lodges in the bèi shū (背俞) vessels, then the vessels become constricted.
If the vessels become constricted, then the blood becomes deficient.
If the blood becomes deficient, then there is pain.
Its shū (俞) point infuses into the heart.
Therefore, they attract each other and cause pain.
Pressing on it brings hot qì (熱氣).
When hot qì (熱氣) arrives, the pain stops.
When cold qì (寒氣) lodges in the jué yīn (厥陰) vessel,
the jué yīn (厥陰) vessel
connects to the yīn (陰) organ and is tied to the liver.
When cold qì (寒氣) lodges in the vessel,
then the blood becomes constricted and the vessel becomes tense.
Therefore, the hypochondrium and lower abdomen attract each other and cause pain.
When perverse qì (厥氣) lodges in the yīn gǔ (陰股),
cold qì (寒氣) rises and reaches the lower abdomen.
The blood constricts below and attracts,
Therefore, abdominal pain extends to the yīn (陰) region and inner thigh.
When cold qi (寒氣) lodges between the membrane origins of the small intestine
and within the network vessels
within the blood, the blood stagnates and cannot be poured into the main meridians.
When the blood and qi (血氣) accumulate and cannot flow,
they will form accumulations (積) over time.
When cold qi (寒氣) lodges in the five zàng (五藏) organs,
counterflow ascends upwards,
the yīn qi (陰氣) is exhausted,
and the yáng qi (陽氣) has not yet entered.
Therefore, there is sudden pain and death, and the person loses consciousness.
If the qi (氣) returns,
then they will live.
When cold qi (寒氣) lodges in the intestines and stomach,
counterflow ascends upwards,
hence there is pain and vomiting.
When cold qi (寒氣) lodges in the small intestine,
the small intestine cannot form a cluster,
hence there is diarrhea and abdominal pain.
When hot qi (熱氣) remains in the small intestine,
there is pain in the intestines,
with exuberant heat, parched thirst,
then it becomes hardened, dry, and cannot be discharged,
hence there is pain and obstruction with no passage.
The Dì (帝) said:
These are what are said and can be understood.
39.3 What about seeing and being able to observe?
What about it?
Qíbó said:
"The five viscera and six bowels
all have their assigned areas.
Observe their five colors;
yellow and red indicate heat,
white indicates cold,
blue and black indicate pain.
These are what are called things that can be seen by observation."
The Emperor said:
"What about those that can be detected by palpation?"
What about it?
Qíbó said:
"Observe the pulse that governs the disease, if it is firm and replete with blood,
and also areas that are depressed,
all these can be detected by palpation."
39.4. The Emperor said:
"Good. I know that all diseases arise from *qì*.
Anger causes *qì* to rise,
joy causes *qì* to relax,
sorrow causes *qì* to dissipate,
fear causes *qì* to descend,
cold causes *qì* to contract,
heat causes *qì* to leak out,
fright causes *qì* to become disordered,
exertion causes *qì* to be consumed,
pensiveness causes *qì* to stagnate.
When the nine *qì* are not in harmony,
what illnesses arise?
Qíbó
said: "Anger causes the *qì* to rise in rebellion.
In severe cases, it causes vomiting of blood and undigested food in the stools.
Therefore, the *qì* ascends.
Joy causes the *qì* to harmonize and the will to be expressed,
and the *yíng* (nutritive *qì*) and *wèi* (defensive *qì*) to flow smoothly.
Therefore, the *qì* becomes relaxed.
Grief causes the heart *xì* (connections) to tighten,
and the lung lobes to lift up,
so that the upper *jiāo* (burner) is not unblocked,
the *yíng* and *wèi* are not dispersed,
and hot *qì* is trapped in the middle.
Therefore, the *qì* is depleted.
Fear causes the essence to recede;
when it recedes, the upper *jiāo* closes;
when it closes, the *qì* returns inward;
when it returns, the lower *jiāo* becomes distended.
Therefore, the *qì* does not flow.
Cold causes the pores to close;
the *qì* does not flow;
therefore, the *qì* is constricted.
Heat causes the pores to open;
the *yíng* and *wèi* flow freely, and sweat is greatly discharged.
Therefore, the *qì* is dissipated.
Fright causes the heart to have nothing to rely on,
the spirit to have nowhere to return,
If anxieties lack resolution,
then the *qi* becomes disordered.
Exertion causes panting and sweating,
dispersing *qi* both externally and internally,
thus the *qi* is depleted.
Thinking causes the mind to have something to dwell on,
and the spirit to have somewhere to return to.
Upright *qi* lingers without circulating,
thus the *qi* becomes stagnant.
Chapter Forty: On the Abdomen
40.1 Huángdì asked:
"There is a disease where the heart and abdomen are full,
and if one eats in the morning, one cannot eat in the evening.
What is this disease?"
Qíbó replied:
"It is called tympanites."
Huángdì said:
"How is it treated?"
Qíbó said:
"Treat it with a dose of chicken-dung liquor; one dose will bring relief, two doses will cure it."
Huángdì said:
"What if it recurs at times?"
Qíbó said:
"This is because of immoderate eating and drinking,
so the disease occurs at times.
Although the disease has subsided,
it will still occur at times,
The *qì* gathers in the abdomen.
40.2 The Emperor asked:
"There is a disease with distention in the chest and hypochondria,
hindering eating.
When the disease arrives, one first smells a fishy and rank odor,
discharges clear fluid,
first spits blood,
has cold extremities,
has dizziness,
and sometimes bleeds before or after defecation.
What is the name of this disease?
How does one contract it?"
Qíbó said:
"The disease is called blood depletion (*xuè kū*).
One contracts this in youth
by having a major loss of blood,
or entering a sexual chamber while drunk.
*Qì* is exhausted and the liver is injured,
therefore menstruation declines and does not come."
The Emperor asked:
"How to treat it?
And what technique to use?"
Qíbó said:
"Use four cuttlefish bones and one *lǘ rú*, combine these two things,
make them into pills with sparrow eggs,
as big as small beans.
Give him abalone juice to drink;
it benefits the intestines and injuries to the liver.
40.3 The Dì [Emperor] said:
"There is a disease with fullness in the lower abdomen,
with roots extending in all directions, up, down, left, and right.
What is this disease,
and is it treatable?" Qíbó said:
"The disease is called Fúliáng (伏梁)."
The Dì [Emperor] said:
"How does Fúliáng arise?"
Qíbó said:
"It is a collection of large amounts of pus and blood
located outside the intestines and stomach.
It is untreatable;
if treated,
each incision and pressure will lead to death."
The Dì [Emperor] said:
"Why is that?"
Qíbó said:
"If below, it will inevitably cause the discharge of pus and blood downwards.
If above, it will press on the stomach and cause obstruction.
Enclosing the stomach may lead to internal abscesses.
This is a long-term illness and difficult to treat.
If located above the navel, it is adverse;
if located below the navel, it is compliant.
Do not move it hastily;
the discussion is in the section on acupuncture methods."
The Emperor said:
"Some people have swelling in their body, thighs, buttocks, and calves,
with pain around the navel.
What is this disease?"
Qíbó said:
"The disease is called Fúliáng.
This is the root of wind.
Its Qi overflows into the large intestine and settles in the *huāng* (region near the navel).
The origin of the *huāng* is below the navel,
therefore there is pain around the navel.
It must not be touched,
touching it will cause the disease of urinary retention."
40.4 The Emperor said:
"You, Master, have often spoken of *rè zhōng* (heat within) and *xiāo zhōng* (wasting and thirsting),
and that it is not advisable to take foods of rich flavor or fragrant herbs and stone-based medicine,
because stone-based medicine can induce epilepsy,
and fragrant herbs can induce madness.
Those with *rè zhōng* and *xiāo zhōng* are all wealthy and noble people,
now if you forbid foods of rich flavor,
this does not suit their desires,
and if you forbid fragrant herbs and stone-based medicine,
the disease will not be cured.
I wish to hear the explanation."
Qíbó said:
"The Qi of fragrant herbs is fine,
the Qi of stone-based medicine is fierce.
The Qi of both is quick, forceful, and strong,
Therefore, one who is not gentle and harmonious cannot subdue these two.
The Emperor said:
"If one cannot subdue these two,
why is that so?"
Qíbó said:
"Now, the nature of hot qi is swift and fierce,
and the nature of the medicinal qi is also like that. If the two meet, I fear it will internally injure the spleen.
The spleen is earth and dislikes wood.
One who takes this medicine
should be reassessed on the days of jiǎ and yǐ."
40.5 The Emperor said:
"Good. There is a disease with swelling of the chest, pain in the neck, fullness in the chest, and distention in the abdomen. What disease is this,
and how does one contract it?"
Qíbó said:
"It is called juénì."
The Emperor said:
"How should it be treated?"
Qíbó said:
"If one moxibusts it, it will cause aphonia; if one uses stone needles, it will cause madness. One must wait until the qi converges before it can be treated."
The Emperor said:
"Why is that so?"
When *yáng qì* rises excessively,
and there is a surplus of it above,
moxibustion will cause the *yáng qì* to enter the *yīn*,
and if it enters, it will cause muteness.
Using stone needles will cause the *yáng qì* to become deficient,
and if it is deficient, it will cause madness.
One must wait for the *qì* to coalesce and then treat it,
and then one can make it whole.
40.6. The Emperor said:
Excellent. How does one know that a pregnant woman is about to give birth?
Qíbó said:
The body has illness but no abnormal pulse.
40.7. The Emperor said:
What is it when one has a fever and experiences pain in a certain area?
What is the reason for this?
Qíbó said:
Fever is associated with
the *yáng* channels.
It is due to the movement of the three *yáng* channels.
At Rén Yíng, one *shèng* corresponds to Shào Yáng,
two *shèng* correspond to Tài Yáng,
three *shèng* correspond to Yáng Míng,
which enters *yīn*.
When *yáng* enters *yīn*,
the illness is located in the head and abdomen,
resulting in distension and headache.
The Emperor said:
Good.
Chapter Forty-one: Piercing for Back Pain

puncture its Xi-cleft point in the Taiyang primary channel to bleed,

and the meeting point of the Yīnwéi 陰維.

Beyond the Tài Yáng,

*Fēng Lùn Piān* (Treatise on Wind) Forty-Second
42.1.1 Huángdì asked,
"When wind injures people,
it manifests either as cold and heat,
or as internal heat,
or as internal cold,
or as *lì fēng* (leprosy-like wind),
or as *piān kū* (unilateral paralysis),
or as *fēng bì* (wind blockage).
The diseases are different,
and their names are not the same,
sometimes reaching internally to the five *zàng* and six *fǔ*.
I do not understand their explanation.
I wish to hear your account."
Qíbó replied,
"Wind *qì* lodges in the space between the skin and flesh,
unable to flow internally,
and unable to vent externally.
Wind,
When good conduct changes frequently,
if the skin pores open, one feels a cold shiver;
if they close, one feels hot and stifled.
When it is cold,
one's appetite and intake of food and drink decline.
When it is hot,
it consumes muscle.
Therefore, it makes people feel anxious and unable to eat,
which is called cold and heat.
When wind-qi together with Yángmíng enters the stomach, it follows the channels upward to the inner canthus of the eye.
If the person is fat, the wind-qi cannot be released externally,
resulting in internal heat and yellow eyes.
If the person is thin,
the wind-qi is released externally, causing cold,
resulting in internal cold and tearful eyes.
When wind-qi together with Tàiyáng enters, it travels through all the channel points,
dispersing in the spaces between the muscles,
interfering with the defensive qi (wèi qì).
If its path is obstructed,
it causes the muscles to swell up and develop sores.
When the defensive qi stagnates and does not circulate,
the flesh becomes numb.
Leprosy sufferers have hot swelling due to nutrient qi (róng qì),
and their qi is impure,
causing their nasal septum to decay and their complexion to deteriorate,
and their skin to ulcerate.
If wind-cold lodges in the channels and does not leave,
it is called leprosy wind (lì fēng),
Or it is named cold and heat.
42.1.2 When in spring, *jiǎ* (*甲*) and *yǐ* (*乙*) are harmed by wind, it is called liver wind;
when in summer, *bǐng* (*丙*) and *dīng* (*丁*) are harmed by wind, it is called heart wind;
when in late summer, *wù* (*戊*) and *jǐ* (*己*) are harmed by evil influences, it is called spleen wind;
when in autumn, *gēng* (*庚*) and *xīn* (*辛*) are affected by evil influences, it is called lung wind;
when in winter, *rén* (*壬*) and *guǐ* (*癸*) are affected by evil influences, it is called kidney wind.
When wind attacks the *shū* (*俞*) points of the five viscera and six bowels, it is also called wind of the viscera and bowels.
Each enters through the doorway it attacks;
if it enters, it causes hemiplegia (deviation).
If wind energy ascends along the *fēng fǔ* (*風府*) point,
it causes brain wind;
if wind enters the head system,
it causes eye wind and cold eyes;
if one consumes alcohol and is struck by wind,
it causes dripping wind;
if one engages in sexual activity with sweating and is struck by wind,
it causes internal wind;
if one is struck by wind after newly bathing, it causes head wind;
if long-term wind enters internally,
it causes intestinal wind with undigested food in the stool;
if it is externally in the *còu lǐ* (*腠理*),
it causes draining wind.
Therefore, wind
is the chief of a hundred diseases.
As for its transformations,
it then becomes other diseases.
There is no constant pattern,
However, it can lead to the formation of wind conditions.
42.2 The Emperor asked:
"Why are the manifestations of wind in the five zàng organs different?
I wish to hear about their diagnosis and the resulting illnesses."
Qíbó said:
"The manifestation of lung wind is:
profuse sweating, aversion to wind,
complexion pale and white,
frequent coughs and shortness of breath,
better during the daytime,
worse in the evening.
The diagnosis is made by observing the area above the eyebrows,
where the color is white.
"The manifestation of heart wind is:
profuse sweating, aversion to wind,
anxiety, agitation, proneness to anger, and fright.
The complexion is red.
When the illness is severe, speech is incoherent.
The diagnosis is made by observing the mouth,
where the color is red.
"The manifestation of liver wind is:
profuse sweating, aversion to wind,
proneness to sadness, complexion slightly pale,
dry throat, proneness to anger,
and frequent dislike of women.
The diagnosis is made by observing the area below the eyes,
where the color is green.
The symptoms of Spleen Wind are:
profuse sweating and aversion to wind,
lassitude of the body,
reluctance to move the four limbs,
a thin, slightly yellow complexion,
poor appetite.
The diagnosis is on the nose,
where the color is yellow.
The symptoms of Kidney Wind are:
profuse sweating and aversion to wind,
a puffy, swollen face,
back pain with inability to stand upright,
the complexion is dark like soot,
hidden areas are constricted and uncomfortable.
The diagnosis is on the skin,
where the color is black.
The symptoms of Stomach Wind are:
profuse sweating and aversion to wind in the neck area,
difficulty in eating and drinking,
obstruction and blockage in the diaphragm,
frequent abdominal distension,
becoming bloated when clothing is removed,
diarrhea after consuming cold food.
The diagnosis reveals a thin body with a large abdomen.
The symptoms of Head Wind are: profuse sweating and aversion to wind in the head and face. One day before the wind [strikes],
the illness becomes severe, with unbearable headache,
exacerbated by going out or staying in until the day of the wind,
then the illness subsides slightly.
The manifestation of *lòu fēng* (wind leakage)
is often excessive sweating,
often being unable to wear a single layer of clothing,
sweating when eating,
and in severe cases, sweating all over the body,
panting and aversion to wind,
clothes constantly damp,
dry mouth and excessive thirst,
and inability to perform laborious tasks.
The manifestation of *xiè fēng* (wind draining)
is excessive sweating,
sweat draining onto clothing,
dryness in the mouth with a coating on the tongue,
inability to perform laborious tasks due to the wind,
and feeling cold with pain all over the body.
The Emperor said:
Good.
Chapter Forty-Three: *Bì Lùn Piān* (Treatise on Impediment)
43.1 The Yellow Emperor asked, saying:
How does *bì* (impediment/numbness) arise?
Qíbó replied, saying:
When wind, cold, and dampness, the three *qì* (energies), arrive together in a mixed state,
they combine to form *bì*.
When the wind *qì* is dominant, it is called *xíng bì* (wandering impediment);
when the cold *qì* is dominant, it is called *tòng bì* (painful impediment);
when the damp *qì* is dominant, it is called *zhuó bì* (fixed impediment).
The Emperor said:
What are these five?
What are they?
Qí Bó said:
Encountering this in winter results in bone bì;
encountering this in spring results in tendon bì;
encountering this in summer results in vessel bì;
encountering this in late yin (long summer) results in muscle bì;
encountering this in autumn results in skin bì.
The Emperor said:
When it resides internally in the five zàng and six fǔ organs,
what qi causes this?
Qí Bó said:
The five zàng all have associating illnesses;
if they persist for a long time and do not depart,
they reside internally in their associations.
Therefore, if bone bì does not resolve,
and one is again affected by evil,
it resides internally in the Kidney;
if tendon bì does not resolve,
and one is again affected by evil, it resides internally in the Liver;
if vessel bì does not resolve,
and one is again affected by evil, it resides internally in the Heart;
if muscle bì does not resolve,
and one is again affected by evil, it resides internally in the Spleen;
if skin bì does not resolve,
and one is again affected by evil,
it resides internally in the Lung.
So-called bì,
each according to its time,
is severely affected by the qi of wind, cold, and dampness.
43.2 In general, when bì affects the five zàng organs,
in the case of lung bì,
there is vexation, fullness, wheezing, and vomiting.
xīn bì zhě, Heart *bì*:
mài bù tōng, the pulse is not flowing,
fán zé xīn xià gǔ, vexation causes a throbbing sensation below the heart,
bào shàng qì ér chuǎn, sudden upward surge of *qì* with dyspnea,
ài gān shàn yī, dry throat, frequent belching,
jué qì shàng zé kǒng; when counterflow *qì* ascends, there is fear;
gān bì zhě, Liver *bì*:
yè wò zé jīng, startled when lying down at night,
duō yǐn shù xiǎo biàn, drinks excessively, frequent urination,
shàng wéi yǐn rú huái; the upper part feels like being pulled as if embracing something;
shèn bì zhě, Kidney *bì*:
shàn zhàng, prone to distention,
kāo yǐ dài zhǒng, the buttocks are used in place of the heels,
jí yǐ dài tóu; the spine is used in place of the head;
pí bì zhě, Spleen *bì*:
sì zhī jiě duò, the four limbs are relaxed and weak,
fā ké ǒu zhī, coughing with vomiting of fluid,
shàng wéi dà sè; the upper part feels greatly obstructed;
cháng bì zhě, Intestine *bì*:
shù yǐn ér chū bù dé, drinks frequently but cannot expel [fluids],
zhōng qì chuǎn zhēng, the middle *qì* is panting and struggling,
shí fā sūn xiè; frequent occurrence of *sūn xiè* (undigested food in stool);
As for bladder impediment,
(it involves) the lower abdomen and bladder.
Pressing it causes internal pain,
as if doused with hot water.
Urination is difficult,
and clear nasal discharge occurs above.
43.3 As for Yin Qi,
when it is still, the spirit is stored;
when it is agitated, it dissipates.
When eating and drinking are doubled (in excess),
the intestines and stomach are thereby injured.
Excessive Qi causing panting,
impediment accumulates in the lungs;
excessive Qi causing worry and contemplation,
impediment accumulates in the heart;
excessive Qi causing incontinence,
impediment accumulates in the kidneys;
excessive Qi causing exhaustion,
impediment accumulates in the liver;
excessive Qi causing muscle weakness,
impediment accumulates in the spleen.
If the various impediments do not cease,
they also increasingly affect internally.
If the wind Qi is dominant,
the person is more likely to recover.
The Emperor said:
With impediment, at times there are deaths,
Some pains last a long time,
while others are easily relieved.
What is the reason for this?
Qíbó said:
Those that enter the Zàng organs result in death;
those that linger between the tendons and bones cause pain to last a long time;
and those that remain between the skin layers are easily relieved.
43.4 The Dì said:
What about those that lodge in the Six Fǔ organs?
Qíbó said:
This is also due to their diet, drink, and living conditions,
which are the root cause of their illness.
The Six Fǔ organs also each have their Yù points.
When wind, cold, or damp Qi invades their Yù points,
and this corresponds to their diet and drink,
it follows the Yù points and enters,
each lodging in its respective Fǔ organ.
The Dì said:
If treating it with acupuncture,
what should be done?
Qíbó said:
The Five Zàng organs have Yù points,
the Six Fǔ organs have Hé points.
Following the divisions of the channels,
each has its specific points,
and each should be treated according to its excess.
Then the disease will be cured.
43.5 The Emperor asked:
"Can the *yíng* and *wèi* qi also cause *bì* (numbness/obstruction)?"
Qíbó replied:
"The *yíng* is the refined qi of water and grain.
It harmonizes and regulates the five *zàng* organs,
diffuses into the six *fǔ* organs,
and then enters the vessels.
Therefore, it circulates up and down the vessels,
connecting the five *zàng* organs and connecting the six *fǔ* organs.
The *wèi* is the forceful qi of water and grain.
Its qi is swift and flowing,
and it cannot enter the vessels.
Therefore, it circulates within the skin,
between the muscles,
warms the *huāng mó* (membranes around the vital organs),
and scatters in the chest and abdomen.
If its qi is opposed, it causes disease;
if its qi is followed, it heals.
If it does not combine with wind, cold, or dampness,
it will not cause *bì*."
The Emperor said:
"Good. *Bì* can be painful,
or not painful, or without sensation,
or cold,
or hot,
or dry,
or damp.
Or damp,
what is the reason for this?
Qí Bó said:
Pain indicates
an abundance of cold qi;
there is cold, therefore there is pain.
As for those that are painless and without sensation,
the disease has been long-standing and has penetrated deeply.
The circulation of *róng* and *wèi* is obstructed.
The channels and collaterals are occasionally sparse,
therefore they are not unobstructed,
and the skin is not nourished,
therefore it becomes without sensation.
As for those that are cold,
*yáng* qi is deficient,
*yīn* qi is abundant,
which mutually increases the disease,
therefore it is cold.
As for those that are hot,
*yáng* qi is abundant,
*yīn* qi is deficient,
the disease qi overcomes the *yáng* and encounters the *yīn*,
therefore it becomes heat *bì*.
As for those that sweat a lot and are wet,
this is due to encountering severe dampness.
*Yáng* qi is deficient,
*yīn* qi is flourishing,
the two qi mutually influence each other,
Therefore, sweat comes out and moistens.
The Emperor asked:
"As for the disease *bì*,
why is there no pain?"
Qíbó said:
"If *bì* is in the bones, there will be heaviness;
if it is in the vessels, the blood will congeal and not flow;
if it is in the tendons, there will be inability to bend and stretch;
if it is in the flesh, there will be numbness;
if it is in the skin, there will be coldness.
Therefore, if all five of these are present,
there will be no pain."
All types of *bì*
encounter cold and contract,
encounter heat and relax.
The Emperor said:
"Good."
Treatise on Flaccidity, Chapter Forty-Four
44.1 The Yellow Emperor asked, "The five viscera cause flaccidity in people, why is that?"
Qíbó replied, "The lungs govern the skin and body hair,
the heart governs the blood vessels of the body,
the liver governs the sinews and membranes of the body,
the spleen governs the muscles of the body,
and the kidneys govern the bones and marrow of the body.

Therefore, if the lungs are hot and the leaves are scorched, then the skin and body hair will be weak and deficient. If pressure is applied hastily and thinly, then flaccidity and paralysis will occur.
If the heart *qì* is hot,
then the lower vessels will rebel and rise upwards;
if the upper vessels rise upwards, then the lower vessels will become deficient.
When they are deficient, then vessel-flaccidity arises,
with dislocated pivot and impaired lifting,
and the shin becomes lax and unable to support the ground.
When the Liver Qi is heated,
then the Gallbladder leaks, the mouth becomes bitter, and the sinews and membranes become dry.
When the sinews and membranes are dry, then the sinews become tense and constricted,
developing into sinew-flaccidity.
When the Spleen Qi is heated,
then the Stomach becomes dry and one thirsts,
and the muscles become insensitive,
developing into muscle-flaccidity.
When the Kidney Qi is heated,
then the loins and spine cannot be raised,
the bones become withered and the marrow diminishes,
developing into bone-flaccidity.
44.2 The Emperor (Dì) asked:
"How does one get it?"
Qíbó replied:
"The Lungs are the chief of the organs,
and serve as the cover for the Heart.
When there is something lost or missing,
or something sought that cannot be obtained,
then the Lungs make a sound.
When they make a sound, then the Lungs are heated and the leaves (of the Lungs) are scorched.
Therefore, it is said:
The five organs, due to the Lungs being heated and the leaves being scorched,
develop into flaccidity and paralysis.
This is what it means.
Excessive grief and sorrow
will sever the perivascular network (bāo luò).
If the perivascular network is severed,
then the *yang* qi moves internally,
resulting in palpitations below the heart and frequent bloody urination.
Therefore, the "Fundamental Diseases" (běn bìng) states:
If the major meridians are empty and deficient,
it gives rise to muscle numbness (jī bì),
which transmits to become pulse flaccidity (mài wěi).
If thoughts are endless,
and what is desired is not obtained,
and the mind wanders excessively outside,
and sexual activity in the bedroom is too excessive,
then the *zong* sinews slacken and become lax,
giving rise to sinew flaccidity (jīn wěi),
and also white emissions (bái yín).
Therefore, the "Lower Classic" (xià jīng) states:
sinew flaccidity (jīn wěi)
arises from the liver's manipulation internally.
If one gradually immerses oneself in dampness and engages in activities involving water,
or if one remains living in a damp place,
When muscles are soaked and macerated,
becoming numb and insensitive,
it manifests as muscle flaccidity (*ròu wěi*).
Therefore, the *Xià Jīng*
says: "Muscle flaccidity (*ròu wěi*),
is acquired from damp ground."
When one travels far and experiences fatigue,
encountering great heat and thirst,
thirst causes the *yáng qì* to internally attack.
Internal attack causes heat to reside in the kidneys.
The kidneys,
are the storage of water.
Now, if water cannot overcome fire,
then the bones become withered and the marrow becomes deficient.
Therefore, the feet cannot support the body,
manifesting as bone flaccidity (*gǔ wěi*).
Therefore, the *Xià Jīng* says,
"Bone flaccidity (*gǔ wěi*),
arises from great heat."
The Emperor asked:
"How can they be distinguished?"
Qí Bó said:
"When the lungs are hot,
the complexion is pale and the hair deteriorates;
when the heart is hot,
the complexion is red and the collaterals overflow;
when the liver is hot,
the complexion is ashen and the nails are dry;
In cases of heat in the spleen,
the complexion is yellow and the flesh twitches.
In cases of heat in the kidneys,
the complexion is black and the teeth are dry.
44.3 The Dì (Emperor) said:
"What you say, Master, is agreeable.
The *Lùn* (Discourse) states that treating flaccidity (wěi) uniquely selects the Yángmíng meridian, why is this so?"
Qíbó said:
"The Yángmíng is
the sea of the five zàng organs and six fǔ organs.
It governs and moistens the general sinews (zōng jīn).
The general sinews govern the binding of the bones and the facilitation of the joints.
The chōng meridian is the sea of the meridians.
It governs the permeation and irrigation of the streams and valleys.
It combines with the Yángmíng at the general sinews.
The Yīn and Yáng converge at the meeting of the general sinews,
meeting at the Qi Street (qì jiē).
And the Yángmíng is their leader.
All belong to the Dài meridian,
and connect to the Dū meridian.
Therefore, when the Yángmíng is deficient, the general sinews become lax,
and the Dài meridian does not support them.
Thus, the foot is flaccid and cannot be used."
The Dì said:
"How should it be treated?"
Qíbó said:
"Supplement their respective yíng points and unblock their shū points,
Regulate their deficiency and excess,
harmonize their opposition and conformity,
sinews, vessels, bones, and flesh,
each according to its season receiving the moon,
then the disease will be cured.
The Emperor said:
Good.
Jué Lùn Chapter Forty-Five
45.1 The Yellow Emperor asked, saying:
What are the cold and heat aspects of *jué*?
Qíbó answered, saying:
When *yáng qì* declines below,
it becomes cold *jué*;
when *yīn qì* declines below,
it becomes heat *jué*.
The Emperor said:
That heat *jué* becomes hot,
and necessarily arises from the soles of the feet,
why is this?
Qíbó said:
*Yáng qì* arises from the exterior of the five toes,
and the *yīn* vessels
gather at the soles of the feet and collect in the center of the foot,
therefore, when *yáng qì* prevails,
the soles of the feet become hot.
The Emperor said:
That cold *jué* becomes cold,
Why must it proceed from the five fingers upwards to the knee?
Qíbó said:
Yīn qì originates from the inside of the five fingers,
gathers below the knee and accumulates above the knee.
Therefore, when Yīn qì prevails,
coldness proceeds from the five fingers to above the knee.
This coldness
does not come from the outside,
but all from the inside.
The Emperor said:
What deficiency causes cold reversal (jué)?
Qíbó said:
The qián yīn (anterior yin, referring to the genitals)
is where the zōng jīn (tendons of the genitals) gather,
and where the tàiyīn (Greater Yin) and yángmíng (Yang Brightness) channels converge.
In spring and summer, yáng qì is abundant and yīn qì is deficient.
In autumn and winter, yīn qì is flourishing and yáng qì is declining.
If a person is physically strong,
but in autumn and winter is depleted by exertion,
the qi struggling upwards from below cannot recover.
The jīng qì overflows downwards,
and evil qi takes the opportunity to follow it upwards.
The qì is due to deficiency within,
yáng qì declines
and cannot nourish its channels.
Yáng qì diminishes daily,
and only yīn qì remains.
Therefore, the hands and feet become cold.
The Emperor asked:
"What causes hot *jue* (reversal)?"
Qíbó said:
"When alcohol enters the stomach,
the *luo* (collateral) vessels become full and the *jing* (channel) vessels become empty.
The spleen is responsible for transporting the fluids of the stomach.
When *yin* (陰) *qi* (氣) is deficient,
then *yang* (陽) *qi* (氣) enters.
When *yang* (陽) *qi* (氣) enters,
then the stomach becomes imbalanced.
When the stomach becomes imbalanced,
then the essential *qi* (氣) is exhausted.
When the essential *qi* (氣) is exhausted,
then it does not nourish the four limbs.
This person must frequently enter sexual activity drunk or after being full.
The *qi* (氣) accumulates in the spleen and cannot be dispersed.
The alcohol *qi* (氣) and the grain *qi* (氣) clash,
heat flourishes in the center,
therefore heat spreads throughout the body, causing internal heat and red urine.
Furthermore, alcohol *qi* (氣) is vigorous and fierce,
and kidney *qi* (氣) declines.
Yang (陽) *qi* (氣) alone prevails,
therefore the hands and feet become hot.
The Emperor asked:
"Some *jue* (reversal) causes abdominal distension,
some causes sudden unconsciousness,
and some cause a person to regain consciousness after half a day, or even a full day.
What is the reason for this?
Qí Bó said:
When *yīn qì* is excessive above, then the lower part becomes deficient;
when the lower part is deficient, then the abdomen becomes distended and full.
When *yáng qì* is excessive above,
then the lower *qì* rises heavily upwards and perverse *qì* rebels.
When it rebels, then the *yáng qì* becomes disordered.
When the *yáng qì* becomes disordered, then one becomes unconscious.
45.2 The Dì (Emperor) said:
Good. I wish to hear about the *jué* manifestations and disease capabilities of the six meridians.
Qí Bó said:
The *jué* of Jùyáng [Greater Yang]
results in swelling of the head, heaviness of the head,
and inability to walk,

The *jué* of Yángmíng [Yang Brightness]

pain in the hypochondrium,
and the hip cannot be moved.
The *jué* of Tàiyīn [Greater Yin]
results in abdominal fullness and distention, difficulty with defecation, a lack of appetite,
vomiting after eating, and inability to lie down.
The *jué* of Shǎoyīn [Lesser Yin]
Then the mouth is dry and the urine is red,
the abdomen is full and the heart hurts.
*Juéyīn*'s *jué* (reversal),
then the lower abdomen is swollen and painful,
the abdomen is distended and the flow of urine is sluggish,
one prefers to lie down with knees bent,
the penis shrinks and swells, with internal heat.
If there is excess, drain it;
if there is deficiency, tonify it;
if there is neither excess nor deficiency,
treat it with redness (i.e., stimulate blood flow).
*Tàiyīn* counterflow,
the penis is tight and cramped,
heart pain extending to the abdomen,
treat the primary disease.
*Shǎoyīn* counterflow,
there is deficient fullness with vomiting and change,
and clear diarrhea,
treat the primary disease.
*Juéyīn* counterflow,
there are spasms and low back pain,
deficient fullness, anterior blockage, and delirious speech,
treat the primary disease.
If the three *yīn* (channels) all have counterflow,
one cannot defecate or urinate,
causing the person's hands and feet to be cold,
and death occurs in three days.
*Tàiyáng* counterflow,
Stiff prostration, vomiting blood, and frequent nosebleeds,
treat the primary disease;
*Shaoyang* reversal,
the joints are dysfunctional,
when the joints are dysfunctional,
the waist cannot move,
the neck cannot turn,
if intestinal carbuncles develop, incurable, death for those who are startled,
*Yangming* reversal, panting cough, body heat,

*Hand Taiyin* reversal,

*Hand Pericardium Shaoyin* reversal,

Chapter 46: On the Capacity for Disease
46.1 The Yellow Emperor asked:
If a person suffers from a carbuncle of the stomach cavity,
How should one diagnose it?
Qí Bó replied:
When diagnosing this,
one should examine the stomach pulse.
The pulse should be deep and thin.
A deep and thin pulse indicates counterflow of qi.
Counterflow
means the Rényíng pulse is very full.
Very full indicates heat.
The Rényíng pulse is the stomach pulse.
Counterflow and fullness
means heat accumulates at the pit of the stomach and does not circulate.
Therefore, the pit of the stomach develops an ulcer.
46.2 The Emperor said:
Good. Why are some people restless when lying down?
Qí Bó said:
If a Zàng organ is injured,
or the essence has a place to lodge, it will be at peace.
Therefore, people cannot suspend their illness.
46.3 The Emperor said:
Why are some people unable to lie on their back?
Qí Bó said:
The lungs
are the cover of the Zàng organs.
If the lung qi is abundant, then the pulse is large.
If the pulse is large, the patient cannot lie down.
The discussion is in "Qí Héng Yīnyáng Zhōng" (奇恒陰陽中).
46.4 The Dì (帝) said:
"If there is a patient with Jue (厥) disease,
and the diagnosis shows the right pulse to be deep and tight,
while the left pulse is floating and slow,
otherwise, where is the primary location of the disease?"
Qíbó (歧伯) said:
"In winter, it is appropriate for the right pulse to be deep and tight,
this corresponds to the four seasons.
The left pulse being floating and slow
is contrary to the four seasons.
If it is on the left, it should indicate the disease is in the kidneys,
somewhat related to the lungs,
and should be manifested as lower back pain."
The Dì (帝) said:
"Why do you say that?"
Qíbó (歧伯) said:
"The Shàoyīn (少陰) meridian traverses the kidneys and connects with the lungs.
Now, obtaining the lung pulse,
the kidneys become diseased because of it,
therefore, the kidneys are the cause of lower back pain."
46.5 The Dì (帝) said:
"Good. If there is a patient with a neck carbuncle,
some treat it with stones,
others treat it with acupuncture and moxibustion,
And all are finished,
where does the truth lie?
Qí Bó said:
These are cases of the same name but different categories.
For those where the *yōng* (carbuncle) *qì* is weak,
it is appropriate to open and remove it with needles;
for those where *qì* is abundant and blood is accumulated,
it is appropriate to drain it with stone needles.
This is what is meant by "same disease, different treatment."
46.6 The Emperor said:
In cases of disease with angry madness, where does this disease arise?
Qí Bó said:
It arises from *yáng*.
The Emperor said:
How does *yáng* cause people to be mad?
Qí Bó said:
*Yáng qì* is easily broken violently and is difficult to resolve,
therefore, they are prone to anger;
the disease is called *yáng jué* (yang reversal).
The Emperor said:
How does one know this?
Qí Bó said:
The *yáng míng* channel is always moving,
the *jù yáng* and *shǎo yáng* channels are not moving,
if they are not moving but suddenly move, it is a great illness;
this is the indication.
The Emperor said:
How should it be treated?
Qíbó 岐伯 said:
Deprive him of food, and it will stop.
For food enters the *yīn*,
and nourishes the *qì* in the *yáng*.
Therefore, deprive him of food, and it will stop.
Make him drink water with filings of raw iron.
Raw iron filings,
are quick to lower the *qì*.
46.7 The Emperor said:
Good. There is a disease with bodily heat that dissipates,
sweating as if from a bath,
aversion to wind and shortness of breath.
What disease is this?
Qíbó 岐伯 said:
The disease is called "wine wind."
The Emperor said:
How should it be treated?
Qíbó 岐伯 said:
Use ten parts each of Zéxiè 澤瀉 (Alisma) and Zhú 朮 (Atractylodes),
and five parts of Míxián 麋銜 (Lysimachia christinae),
mix them, and take three-finger pinch as a post-meal remedy.
46.8. What is meant by "deep and fine"
is that within it, the hand feels like a needle;
rubbing it and pressing it,
that which is gathered is firm;
Bó zhě dà yě. (博者大也。) Broadness means extensiveness.
Shàng jīng zhě, (上經者,) The *shàng jīng* (上經, Upper Classic)
yán qì zhī tōng tiān yě, (言氣之通天也,) speaks of the flow of *qì* that connects with Heaven.
xià jīng zhě, (下經者,) The *xià jīng* (下經, Lower Classic)
yán bìng zhī biànhuà yě, (言病之變化也,) speaks of the transformations of disease.
Jīn Guì zhě, (金匱者,) The *Jīn Guì* (金匱, Golden Cabinet)
jué sǐ shēng yě, (決死生也,) determines life and death.
kuí dù zhě, (揆度者,) *Kuí dù* (揆度) means
qiē dù zhī yě, (切度之也,) to carefully measure and assess it.
Qí Héng zhě, (奇恒者,) *Qí Héng* (奇恒)
yán qí bìng yě. (言奇病也。) speaks of unusual diseases.
Suǒwèi qí zhě, (所謂奇者,) The so-called *qí* (奇, unusual) means
shǐ qí bìng bùdé yǐ sì shí sǐ yě, (使奇病不得以四時死也,) that unusual diseases do not lead to death according to the four seasons.
Héng zhě déyǐ sì shí sǐ yě. (恒者得以四時死也。) *Héng* (恒, normal) means that death may occur according to the four seasons.
Suǒwèi kuí zhě, (所謂揆者,) The so-called *kuí* (揆, assessment) means
fāng qiē qiú zhī yě, (方切求之也,) to seek it by carefully examining the methods,
yán qiē qiú qí mài lǐ yě, (言切求其脈理也,) specifically, to carefully seek its pulse patterns.
Dù zhě dé qí bìng chù, (度者得其病處,) *Dù* (度, measurement) means to determine the location of the disease,
yǐ sì shí dù zhī yě. (以四時度之也。) and to measure it in relation to the four seasons.
Qí Bìng Lùn Piān Dì Sìshíqī (奇病論篇第四十七) Chapter Forty-Seven: Treatise on Strange Diseases
47.1 Huángdì wèn yuē: (黃帝問曰:) The Yellow Emperor asked:
rén yǒu zhòng shēn, (人有重身,) "A woman is pregnant
jiǔ yuè ér yīn, (九月而瘖,) and becomes mute in the ninth month.
cǐ wéi hé yě. (此為何也。) What is the reason for this?"
Qíbó duì yuē: (歧伯對曰:) Qíbó (歧伯) replied:
bāo zhī luò mài jué yě. (胞之絡脈絕也。) "It is due to the severance of the *luò* (絡, connecting) vessel of the uterus."
Dì yuē: (帝曰:) The Emperor said:
How is this explained?
Qí Bó said:
The *bāo luò* (uterus network) is connected to the kidneys;
the *shǎo yīn* meridian
penetrates the kidneys and connects to the root of the tongue,
therefore one cannot speak.
The Emperor said:
How should it be treated?
Qí Bó said:
There is no treatment;
it will recover after ten months.
The method of needling states:
Do not deplete deficiency,
or augment excess,
so as to allow the rash to form,
and then regulate it.
What is meant by not depleting deficiency is,
if the body is weak and emaciated,
there is no use for *chán shí* (large needles);
what is meant by not augmenting excess is,
if there is a tangible mass in the abdomen and one drains it,
draining it will cause the essence to be expelled and the disease will solely dominate the middle,
therefore it is said that the rash will form.
47.2 The Emperor said:
If there is fullness and *qì* rebellion under the ribs,
and it persists for two or three years,
what disease is this?
Qí Bó said:
The name of the disease is called Xī Jī (息積).
This does not affect eating,
and cannot be treated with moxibustion or acupuncture.
For accumulations, use guidance and breathing exercises (dǎo yǐn) and medicine.
Medicine alone cannot cure it.
47.3 The Dì (帝) asked:
Some people have swelling in their body, thighs, and legs,
with pain around the navel. What disease is this?
Qí Bó said:
The name of the disease is called Fú Liáng (伏梁).
This is a wind root.
Its Qi overflows into the large intestine
and attaches to the huāng (肓) area.
The origin of the huāng is below the navel,
therefore there is pain around the navel.
It should not be moved.
If it is moved,
it will cause the disease of difficult and obstructed urination.
47.4 The Dì (帝) asked:
Some people have a very rapid cù (尺) pulse,
with tendons that are tight and visible.
What disease is this?
Qí Bó said:
This is called zhěn jīn (疹筋).
Such a person’s abdomen must be tense.
When white and black (complexion) are seen,
then the disease is severe.
47.5 The Emperor asked:
"There are people who suffer from headaches that persist for several years.
How does this come about,
and what is the name of this disease?"
Qíbó said:
"They must have been exposed to severe cold,
which penetrated to the bone marrow.
The marrow takes the brain as its primary part.
Reversal in the brain therefore causes headaches,
and toothaches as well.
The name of the disease is called *jué nì* (reversal disorder)."
The Emperor said:
"Good."
47.6 The Emperor asked:
"There are people who have a sweet taste in their mouths.
What is the name of the disease,
and how does it come about?"
Qíbó said:
"This is the overflow of the five *qì*,
and it is called *pí dàn* (spleen heat).
When the five flavors enter the mouth,
they are stored in the stomach.
The spleen is responsible for circulating their essence and *qì*.
Fluids and humors are in the spleen,
Therefore, it causes the mouth to taste sweet.
This is the origin of fat and richness.
This person must frequently eat sweet and rich foods and have much fat.
Fat causes internal heat.
Sweetness causes fullness in the middle.
Therefore, their Qi overflows upward
and transforms into wasting and thirsting.
Treat it with *lán* (蘭, orchid/Eupatorium)
to eliminate stale Qi.
47.7 The Emperor asked:
There is a disease where the mouth is bitter.
Take Yánglíng Quán (陽陵泉).
What is the name of the disease where the mouth is bitter?
How does one get it?
Qíbó (歧伯) said:
The name of the disease is Dǎn Dān (膽癉, Gallbladder Jaundice).
The liver is the general in the middle;
it makes decisions based on the gallbladder.
The throat is its messenger.
This person
