Therefore, the gallbladder is deficient and Qi overflows upward,
causing the mouth to be bitter.
Treat it with the gallbladder's *mù* (募) and *shū* (俞) points.
The treatment lies in the relationships of the Yin and Yang twelve officials.
47.8 The Emperor asked:
There is a person with *lóng* (dysuria),
urinating dozens of times a day,
this is deficiency;
the body is hot like charcoal,
the neck and chest are as stiff as if blocked,
the Rén Yíng (人迎) pulse is agitated and exuberant,
breathing is labored and the Qi flows in reverse,
this is excess;
if the Tàiyīn (太陰) pulse is faint and thin like a hair,
this is deficiency.
Where is the disease located,
and what is the name of the disease?
Qíbó (歧伯) said:
The disease is located in the Tàiyīn (太陰),
its excess is in the stomach and somewhat in the lungs,
the disease is called *jué* (厥, collapse),
and is incurable, leading to death.
This is what is meant by obtaining five excesses and two deficiencies.
The Emperor said:
What is meant by "five excesses"
and "two deficiencies"?
Qíbó (歧伯) said:
What is meant by "five excesses" is that the Qi of five diseases is in excess;
"two deficiencies"
also refers to the deficiency of the Qi of the disease.
Now, externally, obtaining five excesses, and internally, obtaining two deficiencies,
the body is neither in the exterior nor in the interior,
and death is clearly evident.
47.9 The Emperor said:
When a person is born with the disease *diān jí* (epilepsy),
what is the name of the disease,
and how does one contract it?
Qíbó said:
The disease is called "fetal illness."
This is contracted while in the mother's womb.
At that time, the mother experienced a great fright,
causing the *qì* to rise and not descend.
The *jīng qì* (essence) resides together,
therefore, it causes the child to develop *diān jí*.
47.10 The Emperor said:
There is a disease that feels as if there is water,
when the pulse is taken, it is large and taut.
The body has no pain,
the form does not thin, and one cannot eat.
One eats little,
what is the name of this disease?
Qíbó said:
The disease originates in the kidney,
and is called kidney wind (*shèn fēng*).
Kidney wind causes one to be unable to eat and prone to fright.
After being frightened,
if the heart *qì* weakens, the person will die.
The Emperor said:
Good.
Dà Qí Lùn Piān Dì Sìshíbā
48.1.1 If the Liver is full, the Kidney is full, and the Lung is full, all being replete,
this becomes swelling.
Lung blockage [leads to] dyspnea and fullness in both hypochondria;
Liver blockage [leads to] fullness in both hypochondria;
lying down causes startle,
and inability to urinate;
Kidney blockage [leads to] fullness from the feet up to at least the lower abdomen,
the lower leg has varying size,
the hipbone is large, lameness,
easily hemiplegia.
48.1.2 If the Heart vessel is full and large,
it is epilepsy and muscular contracture.
If the Liver vessel is small and tense,
it is epilepsy and muscular contracture.
If the Liver vessel is rapid and violent,
there is something frightening,
and if the pulse does not arrive, as if mute,
it will resolve itself without treatment.
If the Kidney vessel is small and tense,
if the Liver vessel is small and tense,
if the Heart vessel is small and tense,
and if they are not drumming, all become masses.
If the Kidney and Liver [pulses] are both deep, it is shí shuǐ (stone-like edema);
if both are floating, it is fēng shuǐ (wind-like edema);
if both are vacuous, it is death;
bìng xiǎo xuán yù jīng.
48.1.3 A kidney pulse that is large, urgent, and deep;
a liver pulse that is large, urgent, and deep;
both indicate shàn (疝, hernia-like conditions).
A heart pulse that throbs rapidly and slippery indicates heart shàn.
A lung pulse that is deep and throbbing indicates lung shàn.
When the three Yang pulses are urgent, it indicates jiǎ (瘕, abdominal masses).
When the three Yin pulses are urgent, it indicates shàn (疝).
When the two Yin pulses are urgent, it indicates xiánjué (癇厥, epilepsy-like seizures).
When the two Yang pulses are urgent, it indicates jīng (驚, fright, convulsion).
48.1.4 A spleen pulse that is bulging outwards
and deep indicates cháng pì (腸澼, dysentery).
It will resolve on its own after a long time.
A liver pulse that is small and moderate indicates cháng pì that is easy to treat.
A kidney pulse that is small and throbbing
and deep indicates cháng pì.
If there is bleeding from below with warm blood and a fever, the person will die.
Heart and liver bì (澼, dysentery) also involve bleeding from below.
If the two organs are diseased together, it is treatable.
If the pulse is small, deep, and hesitant, it indicates cháng pì.
If the body is hot, the person will die.
If the heat appears for seven days, the person will die.
48.1.5 A stomach pulse that is deep, bulging, and hesitant, or a stomach area that is bulging and large;
a heart pulse that is small, firm, and urgent;
both indicate gé piān kū (膈偏枯, hemiplegia).
If a man's left side becomes paralyzed,
and a woman's right side becomes paralyzed,
if they are not mute and their tongues can still move,
it can be treated.
Recovery begins in thirty days.
If the follower (i.e., the condition) causes muteness,
recovery begins in three years.
If the person is under twenty years old,
they will die in three years.
48.1.6 If the pulse arrives and throbs violently,
and there is epistaxis (nosebleed) and fever, the patient will die.
A pulse that comes like a suspended hook, floating, is a normal pulse.
A pulse that arrives like panting is called sudden collapse (bào jué).
Sudden collapse
means the patient does not know how to speak with people.
A pulse that arrives rapidly
causes a person to be suddenly frightened.
It resolves itself in three or four days.
48.2 A pulse that arrives floating and confluent,
a floating and confluent pulse that is rapid,
reaching ten or more beats per breath,
indicates that the channel qi is insufficient.
If subtly apparent, death will occur in ninety days.
A pulse that arrives like burning firewood
indicates that the heart essence is being plundered;
death will occur when the grass dries.
The pulse arriving like scattered leaves,
indicates that the liver *qì* (氣) is in a state of exhaustion;
like wooden leaves falling and dying.
The pulse arriving like greeting a guest,
"Greeting a guest" means,
the pulse is blocked and drumming,
indicates that the kidney *qì* (氣) is in a state of deficiency;
like jujube flowers hanging away and dying.
The pulse arriving like a mud ball indicates that the stomach essence is in a state of insufficiency;
like elm pods falling and dying.
The pulse arriving like a horizontal lattice,
indicates that the gallbladder *qì* (氣) is in a state of insufficiency;
like grain ripening and dying.
The pulse arriving like a string,
indicates that the uterine essence is in a state of insufficiency;
if the patient likes to talk,
they will die when frost falls,
if they do not talk, they can be treated.
The pulse arriving like intertwined lacquer,
"Intertwined lacquer" means,
arriving from both sides,
slightly seen, death will occur within thirty days.
The pulse arriving like a gushing spring, floating and drumming,
indicates that the *tàiyáng qì* (太陽氣) in the muscles is in a state of insufficiency;
if there is little sense of taste,
they will die when the chive flowers bloom.
The pulse arriving in the shape of collapsing earth,
pressing on it yields nothing,
This is the deficiency of *jī qì* (肌氣, muscle Qi).
If the five colors (of the face) first show black and white, and pile up like ramparts, death is imminent.
If the pulse arrives like a hanging uvula,
"hanging uvula" means floating;
if palpating it makes it even larger,
this is the deficiency of the twelve *shū* (俞) points.
Water congeals, and death ensues.
If the pulse arrives like a reclining saber,
"reclining saber" means
floating, small and rapid;
pressing down on it reveals it to be firm, large, and rapid.
The five *zàng* (藏) organs are excessively ripe.
Cold and heat are uniquely combined in the Kidneys.
Such a person cannot sit.
They will die in the first month of Spring.
If the pulse arrives like a smooth, round ball, not straight under the hand,
"not straight under the hand" means
that it cannot be obtained by pressing.
This is the deficiency of the Qi of the Large Intestine.
They will die when the jujube leaves sprout.
If the pulse arrives like a flower,
it makes people prone to fear,
unwilling to sit or lie down,
constantly listening while walking or standing.
This is the deficiency of the Qi of the Small Intestine.
They will die in the late autumn.
Chapter 49: On Pulse Resolution
49.1 The so-called swelling in the waist and pain in the buttocks in Tàiyáng
refers to the first month when Tàiyáng corresponds to Yín.
Yín is Tàiyáng.
In the first month, the yáng qi emerges and rises upward,
while the yīn qi is abundant.
The yáng has not yet reached its proper sequence,
therefore there is swelling in the waist and pain in the buttocks.
The illness where one side is deficient, leading to lameness,
is because in the first month, yáng qi thaws the frozen earth, and the earth qi emerges.
The so-called "one side being deficient" refers to a slight insufficiency during the winter cold.
Therefore, one side being deficient leads to lameness.
The so-called "stiffness extending upwards into the back"
is because the yáng qi rises greatly and contends, hence the stiffness extending upwards.
The so-called "tinnitus"
is because the yáng qi makes all things flourish and leap upwards,
therefore there is tinnitus.
The so-called "severe cases result in mania and convulsions"
is because the yáng is completely at the top,
while the yīn qi is coming from below.
The lower body is deficient, and the upper body is full,
therefore there are mania and convulsions.
The so-called "floating leading to deafness"
all lies in the qi.
The so-called "entering the middle leading to muteness"
is because the yáng is flourishing but already declining,
therefore there is muteness.
Internal depletion leading to cold reversal
results in muteness and aphasia;
This is kidney deficiency.
The *shào yīn* not arriving is
*jué*.
49.2 The *shào yáng* pain of the heart and ribs that is spoken of,
refers to the flourishing of the *shào yáng*.
This flourishing is what is manifested by the heart.
In the ninth month, *yáng qì* is exhausted and *yīn qì* flourishes,
therefore there is pain in the heart and ribs.
What is meant by "unable to turn over"
is that *yīn qì* stores things.
When things are stored, they do not move,
therefore one is unable to turn over.
What is meant by "severe cases may involve leaping"
is that in the ninth month all things wither,
grasses and trees completely shed and fall,
thus the *qì* leaves the *yáng* and goes to the *yīn*.
The *qì* flourishes and the *yáng* grows downward,
therefore it is called leaping.
49.3 The *yáng míng* trembling chills that are spoken of,
*yáng míng*
is *wǔ* (noon),
the *yīn* within the flourishing *yáng* of the fifth month.
*Yáng* flourishes and *yīn qì* is added to it,
therefore there are trembling chills.
What is meant by "swelling of the lower legs but the thighs cannot be drawn up"
is the *yīn* within the flourishing *yáng* of the fifth month.
The *yáng*
declines in the fifth month, and the first *yīn* *qì* rises,
beginning to contend with the *yáng*,
therefore, the lower legs swell and the thighs cannot be drawn up.
The reason for what is called "gasping upwards and resulting in edema"
is that the *yīn* *qì* descends and then ascends again.
Ascending, it invades the spaces between the *zàng* and *fǔ* organs,
therefore, it becomes edema.
The reason for what is called "chest pain with shortness of breath"
is that the water *qì* is in the *zàng* and *fǔ* organs.
Water
is *yīn* *qì*.
When *yīn* *qì* is in the middle,
therefore, there is chest pain and shortness of breath.
The reason for what is called "in severe cases, aversion to people and fire,
and being startled by the sound of wood"
is that *yáng* *qì* and *yīn* *qì* clash with each other,
and water and fire are mutually antagonistic,
therefore, one is startled.
The reason for what is called "wanting to close doors and windows and stay alone"
is that *yīn* and *yáng* are clashing.
When *yáng* is exhausted and *yīn* is flourishing,
therefore, one wants to close doors and windows and stay alone.
The reason for what is called "when the disease arrives, wanting to climb high and sing,
discarding clothes and running away"
is that *yīn* and *yáng* are contending again,
and externally, it combines with *yáng*,
therefore, it causes one to discard clothes and run away.
What is meant by the *kèsūn* branch vessel causing headache, nasal congestion (*bí qiú*), and abdominal distension?
The Yángmíng channel merges upward.
The upward merger
is with its collateral network, the Tài Yīn.
Therefore, it causes headache, nasal congestion (*bí qiú*), and abdominal distension.
49.4 Regarding what the Tài Yīn calls "disease of distension" (*zhàng*),
it is the child of the Tài Yīn.
In the eleventh month, the *qì* of all things is stored within,
therefore it is called "disease of distension."
What is meant by "ascending to the heart, causing hiccuping" (*yī*)
is that Yīn is excessive and ascends to the Yángmíng.
The Yángmíng network connects to the heart,
therefore it is said "ascending to the heart, causing hiccuping."
What is meant by "vomiting after eating"
is that matter is excessive and overflows upward,
therefore one vomits.
What is meant by "feeling better, as if declining, after defecation and expelling gas"
is that in the twelfth month, the Yīn *qì* declines downward,
and the Yáng *qì* is about to emerge,
therefore it is said "feeling better, as if declining, after defecation and expelling gas."
49.5 Regarding what the Shǎo Yīn calls "lower back pain,"
the Shǎo Yīn
is the kidney.
In the tenth month, the Yáng *qì* of all things is injured,
therefore there is lower back pain.
What is meant by "vomiting, coughing, reverse flow of *qì*, and panting"
The *yīn qì* is below,
the *yáng qì* is above.
All the *yáng qì* floats,
with nothing to depend on.
Therefore, there is vomiting, coughing, and shortness of breath.
The so-called "sè sè (colourlessly) unable to stand for long,"
"and when getting up after sitting for a long time, the eyes are *máng máng* (blurred) and see nothing"
is because the *yīn* and *yáng* of all things are unsettled and have no master.
When the *qiū qì* (autumnal energy) first arrives,
and a slight frost first descends,
it then begins to kill all things.
The *yīn* and *yáng* internally seize each other, therefore the eyes are *máng máng* (blurred) and see nothing.
The so-called "having little *qì* and being easily angered"
is because the *yáng qì* is not governed.
If the *yáng qì* is not governed,
then the *yáng qì* cannot escape.
The *gān qì* (Liver Qi) should be governed but is not,
therefore one is easily angered.
Being easily angered
is called *jiān jué* (focal epilepsy).
The so-called "fear, as if someone is about to capture them"
is because in the autumnal *qì*, all things have not completely disappeared.
The *yīn qì* is little,
the *yáng qì* enters,
and the *yīn* and *yáng* attack each other.
Therefore, there is fear.
The so-called "disliking the smell of food"
is because the *wèi* (stomach) has no *qì*.
Therefore, one dislikes the smell of food.
The so-called "face as black as the earth's colour"
is because the autumnal *qì* internally seizes.
Therefore, there is a change in colour.
The so-called "coughing with blood"
is because the *yáng mài* (yang vessel) is injured.
The *yáng qi* is not yet abundant above, yet the vessel is full,
fullness causes coughing,
hence blood is seen in the nose.
49.6 Juéyīn refers to *shān* in the lower abdomen swelling in women,
Juéyīn,
is the *chén* period (7-9 AM),
In the third month, *yáng* within *yīn*, evil residing within,
hence it is said *shān* swelling in the lower abdomen.
The so-called pain in the waist and spine making it impossible to bend forward and backward,
In the third month, everything flourishes and is magnificent,
one bends forward but cannot bend backward.
The so-called retention of urine, *shān*, skin swelling,
is said to be because *yīn* is also flourishing and the vessels are distended and not flowing,
hence it is said retention of urine, *shān*.
The so-called severe cases result in dryness of the throat and internal heat,
is due to *yīn* and *yáng* pressing against each other resulting in heat,
hence the dryness of the throat.
Chapter Fifty: Essential Treatise on Acupuncture
50.1 Huángdì asked,
"I wish to hear about the essentials of acupuncture."
Qí Bó replied,
"Diseases have floating and sinking characteristics,
acupuncture has shallow and deep applications.
Each reaches its principle,
without exceeding its proper course.
Exceeding it causes internal injury,
not reaching it causes external blockage,
and with blockage, evil follows it.
If shallowness and depth are not attained,
it becomes a great robber in reverse,
internally stirring the five zàng organs, later producing serious illness.
Therefore, it is said:
There are diseases located in the fine hairs and interstices of the skin,
some located in the skin,
some located in the muscles,
some located in the vessels,
some located in the tendons,
some located in the bones,
some located in the marrow.
Therefore, when needling the fine hairs and interstices of the skin,
do not injure the skin;
if the skin is injured, it internally stirs the lungs;
if the lungs are stirred, in the autumn it will cause warm malaria,
with shivering and chills.
When needling the skin,
do not injure the flesh;
if the flesh is injured, it internally stirs the spleen;
if the spleen is stirred, in seventy-two days, in the months of all four seasons,
Illness with abdominal distention and vexation,
not desiring food;
puncture flesh,
without injuring the vessels.
If the vessels are injured, then internally the heart stirs;
if the heart stirs, then in summer the illness is heart pain;
puncture vessels,
without injuring the sinews.
If the sinews are injured, then internally the liver stirs;
if the liver stirs, then in spring the illness is heat with sinew laxity;
puncture sinews without injuring bone.
If the bone is injured, then internally the kidneys stir;
if the kidneys stir, then in winter the illness is distention and lower back pain;
puncture bone,
without injuring marrow.
If the marrow is injured, then there is wasting and consumption,
aching shins,
and the body disintegrates and cannot recover.
*Cì Qí Lùn Piān* (On the Principles of Puncturing), Chapter Fifty-One
51.1 The Yellow Emperor asked:
I wish to hear about the distinctions in shallow and deep puncturing.
Qíbó answered:
When puncturing bone, do not injure sinews;
when puncturing sinews, do not injure flesh;
when puncturing flesh, do not injure vessels;
when puncturing vessels, do not injure skin;
when puncturing skin, do not injure flesh;
when puncturing flesh, do not injure sinews;
when puncturing sinews, do not injure bone.
51.2 The Emperor said:
I do not yet know what you mean.
I wish to hear your explanation.
Qíbó said:
"To puncture bone without injuring the sinews"
means the needle reaches the sinews and is withdrawn,
not reaching the bone.
"To puncture sinews without injuring the flesh"
means reaching the flesh and withdrawing,
not reaching the sinews.
"To puncture flesh without injuring the vessels"
means reaching the vessels and withdrawing,
not reaching the flesh.
"To puncture vessels without injuring the skin"
means reaching the skin and withdrawing,
not reaching the vessels.
"To puncture skin without injuring the flesh"
means the disease is within the skin;
the needle enters the skin
without injuring the flesh.
"To puncture flesh without injuring the sinews"
means passing the sinews within the flesh.
"To puncture sinews without injuring the bone"
means passing the bone within the sinews.
This is called contradiction (反 fǎn).
Cì Jìn Lùn Piān Dì Wǔshí'èr
52.1 The Discourse on Prohibitions and Punctures, Chapter Fifty-Two.
The Yellow Emperor asked, "I wish to hear about the prohibited points and numbers."
Qíbó replied, "The viscera have essential points and harms,
which must be carefully examined.
The liver arises on the left,
the lungs are stored on the right,
the heart is manifested on the exterior,
the kidneys govern the interior,
the spleen acts as their messenger,
and the stomach acts as their marketplace.
Above the diaphragm and the *huāng* point,
within, there are the parents;
beside the seven vertebrae,
within, there is the lesser heart.
Following it brings fortune;
opposing it brings misfortune."
52.2 Puncturing the heart results in death in one day;
its symptom is hiccuping.
Puncturing the liver results in death in five days;
its symptom is speech.
Puncturing the kidney results in death in six days;
its symptom is sneezing.
Puncturing the lung results in death in three days;
its symptom is coughing.
Its movement is sneezing (tì).
If you puncture the lungs (fèi) and hit the mark,
death will occur in three days.
Its movement is coughing (ké).
If you puncture the spleen (pí) and hit the mark,
death will occur in ten days.
Its movement is swallowing (tūn).
If you puncture the gallbladder (dǎn) and hit the mark,
death will occur in one and a half days.
Its movement is vomiting (ǒu).
52.3 If you puncture the instep of the foot (fū shàng),
hitting a major vessel,
and the blood flows out without stopping,
death will occur. If you puncture the face (miàn)
and hit the liū vessel,
unfortunately, it will cause blindness (máng).
If you puncture the head (tóu), hitting the nǎohù in the brain,
immediate death will occur.
If you puncture the central vessel under the tongue (shé xià zhōng mài) too deeply,
and the blood flows out without stopping, it will cause muteness (yīn).
If you puncture the network of vessels on the sole of the foot (zú xià bù luò zhōng mài),
and no blood comes out, it will cause swelling (zhǒng).
If you puncture the major vessel in the popliteal fossa (xì zhōng dà mài),
it will cause a person to fall down, losing color.
If you puncture the central vessel of the qì jiē,
and no blood comes out,
it will cause swelling, buboes and falling.
Needling the spine at leisure,
injures the spinal cord, causing kyphosis.
Needling above the nipple,
injures the mammary glands, causing swelling and erosion.
Needling the supraclavicular fossa in the inner depression,
dissipates the *qì*, causing shortness of breath, coughing, and counterflow.
Needling the thenar eminence in the inner depression causes swelling.
Do not needle a person who is very drunk,
as it will cause the *qì* to become disordered.
Do not needle a person who is very angry,
as it will cause the *qì* to flow in reverse.
Do not needle a person who is greatly fatigued,
do not needle a person who is newly full,
do not needle a person who is greatly hungry,
do not needle a person who is greatly thirsty,
do not needle a person who is greatly frightened.
Needling the large vessel in the inner thigh,
if the blood does not stop flowing out,
causes death. Needling the sunken inner pulse of the *kè zhǔ rén* (客主人) point,
causes internal leakage and deafness.
Needling the kneecap causing fluid effusion, results in lameness.
Needling the *tàiyīn* (太陰) vessel of the arm,
with profuse bleeding, causes immediate death.
Needling the *shǎoyīn* (少陰) vessel of the foot,
with excessive depletion and bleeding,
causes difficulty in speaking.
Needling the center of the chest, in the depression, injures the lungs,
causing shortness of breath, counterflow, and upward breathing.
To puncture the inner depression of the elbow
causes the *qì* to return there,
resulting in inability to flex and extend the arm.
To puncture the inner depression three *cùn* below the groin
causes a person to urinate involuntarily.
To puncture the inner depression below the armpit, between the ribs,
causes a person to cough.
To puncture the lower abdomen, causing the bladder to leak urine,
causes a feeling of fullness in the lower abdomen.
To puncture the calf intestine, causing it to sink inward, causes swelling.
To puncture above the eye socket, in the depression of the bone and vessel,
causes leakage and blindness.
To puncture the fluid in the joints
causes inability to flex and extend the limbs.
Chapter 53: On Puncturing and the Spirit [*Zhì Lùn Piān* Dì Wǔshísān]
53.1 The Yellow Emperor [*Huángdì*] asked:
I wish to hear the essentials of deficiency and excess.
Qíbó replied:
When the *qì* is substantial, the form is substantial;
when the *qì* is deficient, the form is deficient.
This is the norm.
Deviation from this is disease.
When grain is abundant, *qì* is abundant;
when grain is deficient, *qì* is deficient.
This is the norm.
Deviation from this is disease.
When the pulse is substantial, the blood is substantial;
When the pulse is deficient and the blood is deficient,
this is the norm;
deviating from this is a sign of disease.
53.2 The Dì (Yellow Emperor) said:
How does it deviate?
Qíbó replied:
When the *qì* is deficient but the body is hot,
this is called a deviation.
When much grain enters but the *qì* is little,
this is called a deviation.
When little grain enters but the *qì* is much,
this is called a deviation.
When the pulse is full but the blood is little,
this is called a deviation.
When the pulse is little but the blood is much,
this is called a deviation.
53.3 When the *qì* is abundant but the body is cold,
it is due to *shānghán* (cold damage).
When the *qì* is deficient but the body is hot,
it is due to *shāngshǔ* (summerheat damage).
When much grain enters but the *qì* is little,
it is due to some blood loss and dampness dwelling below.
When little grain enters but the *qì* is much,
the pathogenic influence is in the stomach, and in the lungs.
When the pulse is small but the blood is much,
there is heat within from drinking.
When the pulse is large but the blood is deficient,
the pulse contains wind-qi.
Water and gruel do not enter.
This is what it means.
53.4 Now, "substantiality"
means the entry of qi.
"Deficiency"
means the exit of qi.
When the qi is substantial,
it is heat.
When the qi is deficient,
it is cold.
"Entering substantiality"
means opening the acupuncture point with the left hand.
"Entering deficiency"
means closing the acupuncture point with the left hand.
Chapter 54: Explanation of Acupuncture
54.1 Huángdì asked,
"I wish to hear the explanation of the Nine Needles and
the principles of deficiency and substantiality."
Qíbó replied,
"To supplement deficiency means to make the needle feel hot beneath it.
The needle feels hot beneath it because the qi is substantial.
It is hot because the qi is substantial.
To drain fullness means to make the needle feel cold beneath it.
The needle feels cold beneath it because the qi is deficient.
Qi Deficiency is cold.
To remove that which is stagnant and old
is to expel bad blood.
If evil prevails, then drain it;
when the needle is out, do not press.
Slow in and fast out makes it full;
slowly withdraw the needle and press quickly.
Fast in and slow out makes it empty;
withdraw the needle quickly and press slowly.
Speaking of fullness and emptiness
refers to the cold, heat, and quantity of Qi.
As if nothing, as if something exists;
the ailment is unknowable.
Examining what comes after and before
is knowing the sequence of the illness.
To treat emptiness and fullness,
the practitioner must not lose the method.
As if gaining, as if losing;
that is departing from the method.
The essentials of emptiness and fullness:
the nine needles are most marvelous
because each has its suitability.
The timing of tonifying and draining
is to accord with the opening and closing of Qi.
The names of the nine needles,
each having a different shape,
the needles exhaustively address what should be tonified and drained.
54.2 When puncturing to reduce excess, one must wait for the depletion of the excess
and retain the needle until the *yīn* *qì* flourishes and arrives,
then remove the needle.
When puncturing to supplement deficiency, one must wait for the fulfillment of the deficiency,
until the *yáng* *qì* flourishes and arrives,
and a feeling of heat arises beneath the needle, then remove the needle.
Once the channel *qì* has arrived,
carefully guard it and do not lose it;
do not change or alter it.
The depth [of insertion] depends on one's intent,
understanding the interior or exterior location of the disease.
Near and far are as one,
meaning the depths [of insertion] and their indications are equivalent.
Like approaching a deep abyss,
one dares not fall.
One's hand should be like grasping a tiger,
desiring strength.
The spirit should not be distracted by external things,
be still and observe the patient, without looking left or right.
Righteousness should not deviate downward,
desiring uprightness and correctness.
One must rectify one's spirit,
intending to observe the patient's eyes to control their spirit,
allowing *qì* to flow easily.

Apply the same method to both the upper and lower parts [of the body].

is called Shū Rú (樞儒).
Apply the same method to both the upper and lower parts [of the body].

56.2 Therefore, the beginning of all diseases,

The skin

Good.

while network vessels have inconstant changes.

The heart is red,
the lungs are white,
the liver is blue,
the spleen is yellow,
the kidneys are black.

The Dì (Emperor) said:
Are the *luò* of *yīn* and *yáng*
also corresponding to their respective *jīng*?
Qíbó said:
The color of the *yīn luò* corresponds to its *jīng*,
the color of the *yáng luò* changes unpredictably,
and follows the four seasons.
When cold is excessive, it congeals and stagnates;
when it congeals and stagnates, it becomes blue-black;
when heat is excessive, it becomes damp and lustrous;
when it is damp and lustrous, it becomes yellow-red.
These are all normal colors,
indicating no disease.
If all five colors are seen,
it indicates cold and heat.

Good.

The Rèn Mài is a channel that

The Chōng Mài is a channel that

If the Rèn Mài is diseased,

When the Dū Vessel (督脈) is diseased,

The Dū Vessel (督脈):

In women, it enters and connects to the Tíngkǒng (廷孔).
That Kǒng (孔),

Its collaterals follow the Yīnqì (陰器), converge in the cuàn jiān (篡閒), and encircle behind the cuàn (篡).
Separately, it circles the buttocks towards the Shàoyīn (少陰),
where it joins with those collateralizing through the Jùyáng (巨陽).
The Shàoyīn (少陰) ascends the inner posterior border of the thigh,

With the Tàiyáng (太陽), it originates from the inner canthus of the eye,

In men, it follows the penis down to the cuàn (篡),
similar to women.
Its branch that ascends directly from the lower abdomen traverses the center of the navel,
ascends and traverses the heart and enters the throat,
ascends to the chin and encircles the lips,
ascends and connects to the center below both eyes.
This causes illnesses that ascend from the lower abdomen, attacking the heart,
with pain preventing forward and backward movement,
which is chōng shàn (衝疝).
suffering from strangury, hemorrhoids, urinary incontinence, or a dry throat,

The treatment is on the bone.
In severe cases, it is located below the Qí (umbilicus) and within the Yíng (营, a place name, possibly referring to a specific point or region).
If the upper *qì* has sound,

If the center is located in the quē pén (缺盆, Supraclavicular Fossa),

Jiàn (漸) is located above, flanking the yí (頤, cheek).
60.2.1 For a bent knee that cannot be extended or flexed, treat its jiàn (楗, pivot).

When standing brings relief from heat,

treat the Shǎo Yáng (少陽, Lesser Yang) channel's wéi (維, junction),

Above the fǔ gǔ (輔骨, accessory bone) and below the héng gǔ (橫骨, transverse bone) is called jiàn (楗, pivot).
The *xiá* (sides of the hip) are the pivot,

It has no marrow holes.

Treatise on the Water-Heat Cavities: Chapter Sixty-One
61.1.1 The Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) asked:
"Why does Shǎoyīn govern the kidney,
and why does the kidney govern water?"
Qíbó replied:
"The kidney
is the ultimate yin.
The ultimate yin
is the storage of water.
The lung
is tàiyīn.
Shǎoyīn
is the winter pulse.
Therefore, its root is in the kidney,
and its extremity is in the lung,
and both accumulate water."
The Emperor said:
"How can the kidney accumulate water and generate disease?"
Qíbó replied:
The kidneys
are the gateway of the stomach.
If the gateway is not functioning properly,
water will accumulate and follow its kind.
If it overflows upwards and downwards into the skin,
it will cause edema.
Edema is
a disease caused by the accumulation of water.
61.1.2 The Dì said:
Do all types of edema originate in the kidneys?
Qíbó said:
The kidneys
are the *pìn zàng* (female storehouse).
The earth *qì* that rises upwards belongs to the kidneys
and generates water and fluids.
Therefore, it is called "supreme *yīn*."
If one is brave and labors excessively, the kidneys will sweat.
If the kidneys sweat and are exposed to wind,
the sweat cannot enter the internal organs,
nor can it escape through the skin.
It lodges in the *xuán fǔ*,
flows beneath the skin,
and transmits into edema.
Originating in the kidneys,
this is called "wind edema" (*fēng shuǐ*).
The so-called *xuán fǔ*
are the sweat pores.
61.1.3 The Emperor asked:
"The water-transporting points, in fifty-seven locations,
what do they govern?"
Qíbó said:
"The kidney-transporting points, in fifty-seven locations,
are where accumulated Yin gathers,
and from where water enters and exits.
On the sacrum, five rows with five points each,
these are the kidney-transporting points.
Therefore, in water diseases,
below, there is swelling of the instep and a large abdomen,
above, there is panting and wheezing,
and inability to lie down.
Both the root and the branch are diseased,
thus the lungs cause panting and wheezing,
and the kidneys cause water swelling.
The lungs cause counterflow, resulting in inability to lie down.
When divided into mutually transporting and jointly receiving,
it is where water qi stagnates.
Above the Fú Tù (lying rabbit) point, two rows with five points each,
these are the streets of the kidney.
Where the three Yin channels converge on the foot.
Above the ankle, one row with six points each,
this is the downward course of the kidney channel,
called Tài Chōng.
All fifty-seven points
are hidden in the Yin collaterals,
Where the water lodges.
61.2 The Emperor said:
In spring, you take from the collaterals and the spaces between muscles,
why is that?
Qí Bó said:
Spring is when
wood begins to govern,
the Liver-qi begins to generate.
The Liver-qi is urgent,
and its wind is swift.
The channels are usually deep,
their qi is little,
and cannot deeply penetrate.
Therefore, one takes from the collaterals and the spaces between muscles.
The Emperor said:
In summer, you take from the abundant channels and the interstices of the skin,
why is that?
Qí Bó said:
Summer is when
fire begins to govern,
the Heart-qi begins to grow.
The vessels are thin, the qi is weak,
the Yang-qi remains and overflows,
heat smolders in the interstices of the skin,
internally reaching the channels.
Therefore, one takes from the abundant channels and the interstices of the skin, severing the skin to remove the illness,
because the evil resides shallowly.
What are called "shèng jīng" (盛經)
are the yáng (陽) vessels.
The Emperor said:
"Why do we take the shū (俞) points of the meridians in autumn?"
Qíbó (歧伯) said:
"Autumn is
when metal begins to govern,
the lungs are about to gather and kill,
metal is about to overcome fire,
yáng qì (陽氣) is in the hé (合) points,
yīn qì (陰氣) initially prevails,
dampness reaches the body,
yīn qì (陰氣) is not yet flourishing,
and cannot penetrate deeply.
Therefore, we take the shū (俞) points to drain away the yīn (陰) evil,
and take the hé (合) points to deplete the yáng (陽) evil.
Yáng qì (陽氣) initially declines,
therefore we take from the hé (合) points."
The Emperor said:
"Why do we take the jǐng (井) and yíng (榮) points in winter?"
Qíbó (歧伯) said:
"Winter is
when water begins to govern,
the kidneys are just closing,
yáng qì (陽氣) is declining and weakening,
yīn qì (陰氣) is firm and flourishing,
the great yáng (巨陽) is hidden and submerged,
and the yáng (陽) vessels then depart.
Therefore, we take the jǐng (井) points to lower the inverse yīn (陰),
and take the yíng (榮) points to replenish the yáng qì (陽氣).
Therefore it is said:
'In winter, take the jǐng (井) and yíng (榮) points.'"
so that in spring one will not suffer from nasal congestion or nosebleeds,
this is what it means.
61.3 The Dì (Emperor) said:
You, Master, spoke of treating febrile diseases with fifty-nine points;
I have considered the meaning of this,
but have not been able to distinguish their locations.
I wish to hear their locations
and consequently understand their meaning.
Qíbó said:
The five rows of five points on the head
are for draining the inverse heat of the various yang channels.
Dàzhù, the ying points, quēpén, and back shù points—these eight points
are for draining the heat in the chest.
Qìjiē, Sānlǐ, Jùxū, the upper and lower lián—these eight points
are for draining the heat in the stomach.
Yúnmén, yúgǔ, wěizhōng, and suǐkōng—these eight points
are for draining the heat in the four limbs.
The five shù points beside the five zàng—these ten points
are for draining the heat in the five zàng organs.
All these fifty-nine acupoints
are on both sides of the heat.
The Dì (Emperor) said:
People injured by cold then transmit to heat,
why is that?
Qíbó said:
When cold is excessive,
then heat is generated.
*Tiáo Jīng Lùn Piān* (Treatise on Regulating the Meridians) Section Sixty-Two
62.1 The Yellow Emperor asked:
I have heard in the discussions on the method of acupuncture that,
"If there is excess, drain it;
if there is deficiency, supplement it."
What is meant by "excess,"
what is meant by "deficiency"?
Qíbó replied:
There are five types of excess,
and five types of deficiency as well.
What is it that you wish to ask about, O Emperor?
The Emperor said:
I wish to hear them all.
Qíbó said:
The *shén* (spirit) has excess and deficiency,
the *qì* has excess and deficiency,
the blood has excess and deficiency,
the form has excess and deficiency,
the will has excess and deficiency.
All these ten things,
their *qì* are not equal.
The Emperor said:
"People have essence, qi, fluids,
four limbs, nine orifices,
five viscera, sixteen departments,
three hundred and sixty-five joints,
which give rise to hundreds of diseases.
The arising of hundreds of diseases
all have conditions of excess and deficiency.
Now, Master, you speak of there being five excesses
and also five deficiencies.
How do these arise?"
Qíbó said:
"They all arise from the five viscera.
The heart stores the spirit (shén),
the lungs store the qi,
the liver stores the blood,
the spleen stores the flesh,
the kidneys store the will (zhì).
And these form the body.
The will (zhì) and intent communicate internally, connecting to the bone marrow,
and form the body and the five viscera.
The way of the five viscera
all emerges from the meridians (jīng suì), in order to circulate the blood and qi.
If the blood and qi are not in harmony,
hundreds of diseases then transform and arise.
Therefore, one should guard the meridians (jīng suì)."
62.2.1 The Emperor said:
What is the condition when the spirit (shén) is in excess or deficient?
Qíbó said:
If the spirit (shén) is in excess, one laughs incessantly.
If the spirit (shén) is deficient, one is sorrowful.
When the blood and qi (qì) have not yet merged,
and the five viscera are stable,
evil invades the form (xíng),
and shivering arises from the fine hairs,
it has not yet entered the meridians and collaterals.
Therefore, it is called the subtlety of the spirit (shén).
The Emperor (Dì) said:
What should be done to supplement or drain it?
Qíbó said:
If the spirit (shén) is in excess,
then drain the blood from its small collaterals,
drawing blood without deeply penetrating.
Do not hit its major meridian,
then the spirit (shén) and qi (qì) will be balanced.
If the spirit (shén) is deficient,
observe its deficient collaterals,
press and guide it,
prick and benefit it,
do not draw out its blood,
do not drain its qi (qì),
in order to unblock its meridian,
then the spirit (shén) and qi (qì) will be balanced.
The Emperor (Dì) said:
How should one needle the subtlety?
Qíbó said:
"When performing massage, do not release [pressure].
When applying acupuncture, do not reject [the needle].
Transfer the *qì* to where it is deficient,
and the spirit-*qì* will then be restored."
62.2.2 The Dì said:
"Good. What about excess and deficiency?"
Qíbó said:
"If *qì* is in excess, then there will be panting and coughing.
If *qì* is insufficient in the upper body,
then there will be rapid breathing and shortness of breath.
If blood and *qì* have not yet combined,
and the five viscera are stable,
and the skin has a slight ailment,
this is called a slight leakage of white *qì*."
The Dì said:
"What about supplementing and draining?"
Qíbó said:
"If *qì* is in excess,
then drain its channels,
without harming its channel,
without drawing out its blood,
without leaking its *qì*.
If deficient,
then supplement its channels,
without drawing out its *qì*."
The Dì said:
How does one needle subtly?
Qíbó said:
Massage without releasing,
withdraw the needle and observe it.
Say, "I will deepen it."
If a person adapts, they will certainly change.
The refined qi naturally submits.
The pathogenic qi scatters and becomes disordered,
having no place to rest.
The qi leaks through the pores,
and true qi is then attained.
62.2.3 The Emperor said:
Good. What about excess or deficiency of blood?
How should it be treated?
Qíbó said:
If there is excess blood, then there is anger.
If there is insufficient blood, then there is fear.
If blood and qi are not combined,
the five organs are stable.
If the minor collaterals overflow with water,
then the meridians will have retained blood.
The Emperor said:
How does one tonify and drain?
Qíbó said:
If there is excess blood,
then drain the full meridian and extract its blood.
If there is deficiency,
Then observe its deficient channels and insert the needle into the midst of its vessels.
Leave it in place for a long time and observe.
If the pulse becomes large,
quickly withdraw the needle,
without letting blood leak out.
The Dì said:
How about puncturing and retaining blood?
What should be done?
Qíbó said:
Observe its blood vessels,
puncture and release its blood,
without allowing impure blood to enter the channels,
thereby causing disease.
62.2.4 The Dì said:
Good. What about excess or deficiency in form?
Qíbó said:
If there is excess in form, then the abdomen will be distended and urination will be difficult.
If there is deficiency, then the four limbs will be unusable.
If blood and *qì* have not yet combined,
the five viscera are stable,
and the muscles are twitching,
this is called a slight wind.
The Dì said:
How about supplementing and draining?
Qíbó said:
If there is excess in form, then drain its *yáng* channels.
If there is deficiency, then supplement its *yáng luò*.
The Emperor said:
How is subtle needling done?
Qíbó said:
Take the spaces between the muscles,
do not hit the meridians,
do not damage the collaterals.
When the defensive qi is restored,
the pathogenic qi will then diminish.
62.2.5 The Emperor said:
Good. What if the will (zhì) is excessive or deficient?
Qíbó said:
If the will is excessive, then there will be abdominal distention and undigested food in the stool;
if it is deficient, then there will be cold reversal (jué).
Blood and qi have not yet combined,
the five organs are stable,
the bones and joints are moving.
The Emperor said:
How do you tonify and drain?
Qíbó said:
If the will is excessive, then drain the sinews and blood;
if it is deficient, then tonify its Fùliū (復溜) point.
The Emperor said:
What if the stabbing is not yet combined?
Qíbó said:
Then take it,
do not hit the meridians,
the pathogenic site can then be made deficient.
62.3 The Emperor said:
"Good. I have already learned about the forms of deficiency and excess,
but I don't know how they arise."
Qíbó said:
"When the qi and blood combine,
and the yīn and yáng lean against each other,
the qì becomes disordered in the wèiqì,
and the blood rebels in the channels,
causing the blood and qì to separate,
resulting in one excess and one deficiency.
When the blood combines with the yīn,
and the qì combines with the yáng,
it results in fright and mania.
When the blood combines with the yáng,
and the qì combines with the yīn,
it results in a feeling of heat within (jiǒngzhōng).
When the blood combines above,
and the qì combines below,
the heart is vexed, and there is grief and frequent anger.
When the blood combines below,
and the qì combines above,
there is confusion and frequent forgetfulness."
The Emperor said:
"When the blood combines with the yīn,
and the qì combines with the yáng,
and the blood and qì separate like this,
which is the excess,
What constitutes emptiness?
Qíbó said:
Blood and Qi,
prefer warmth and dislike cold.
When cold, the blood weeps and cannot flow.
When warm, it dissolves and disperses.
Therefore, where Qi gathers, there is blood deficiency.
Where blood gathers, there is Qi deficiency.
The Emperor asked:
What a person possesses
is blood and Qi.
Now, you, Master, say that blood gathering is emptiness,
and Qi gathering is emptiness.
Is there then nothing substantial?
Qíbó said:
What exists is substantial;
what is absent is emptiness.
Therefore, when Qi gathers, there is no blood.
When blood gathers, there is no Qi.
Now, blood and Qi lose each other,
thus creating emptiness.
The collaterals and minute collaterals all flow into the main channels.
When blood and Qi gather together,
it results in fullness.
When blood and Qi rush together upwards,
it causes a major reversal (jue).
Reversal leads to sudden death.
If the Qi returns, then life is restored.
If you do not reverse it, you will die.
The Emperor said:
"From what path does the substantial come,
and from what path does the insubstantial depart?
The essentials of substantiality and insubstantiality,
I wish to hear the reason for them."
Qí Bó said:
"Now, yin and yang
both have their meeting points.
Yang pours into yin,
yin is full on the outside,
yin and yang are evenly balanced,
so as to fill the body.
The nine pulses are as one;
this is called a normal person."
62.4 Now, the arising of evil
either arises from yin
or arises from yang.
That which arises from yang
is obtained from wind, rain, cold, and heat.
That which arises from yin
is obtained from diet, dwelling place,
yin and yang, joy and anger."
The Emperor said:
"How do wind and rain injure people?"
Qí Bó said:
"When wind and rain injure people,
First, it lodges in the skin;
then it spreads into the *sūn* channels.
When the *sūn* channels are full, it spreads into the *luò* channels.
When the *luò* channels are full, it is transported to the major meridians.
Blood and *qì*, along with the pathogenic factor, lodge in the spaces between the skin and muscles.
The pulse becomes firm and large;
therefore, it is called repletion (*shí*).
Repletion means the exterior is firm and full,
and it cannot be pressed;
pressing it causes pain.
The Emperor asked:
How does cold-dampness harm people?
Qíbó said:
When cold-dampness affects people,
the skin does not contract,
and the muscles become hard and tight.
The *yíng* blood congeals,
and the *wèi* *qì* departs;
therefore, it is called depletion (*xū*).
Depletion means there is a lack of *qì*,
pressing it causes *qì* to sufficiently warm it,
therefore, it feels pleasant and not painful.
The Emperor said:
Good. How does the production of yin repletion occur?
Qíbó said:
If joy and anger are not regulated,
then the yin *qì* rises in reverse.
If it rises in reverse, then the lower body becomes deficient.
When the lower body is deficient, the *yáng qì* escapes downward,
therefore it is said to be substantial.
The Emperor asked:
How does deficiency give rise to *yīn*?
Qíbó said:
Joy causes *qì* to descend,
sorrow causes *qì* to dissipate.
When *qì* dissipates, the pulse becomes deficient and empty.
Due to cold food and drink,
cold *qì* fills and suffuses,
then blood congeals and *qì* departs,
therefore it is said to be deficient.
62.5 The Emperor asked:
The classics say, "When *yáng* is deficient, there is external cold;
when *yīn* is deficient, there is internal heat;
when *yáng* is excessive, there is external heat;
when *yīn* is excessive, there is internal cold."
I have already heard of these,
but I do not know the reasons for them.
Qíbó said:
*Yáng* receives *qì* from the upper *jiāo*,
to warm the skin and the spaces between muscles.
If cold *qì* is on the outside,
then the upper *jiāo* is not unblocked.
If the upper *jiāo* is not unblocked,
then cold *qì* alone remains on the outside,
hence shivering.
The Emperor asked:
"How does *yīn* deficiency generate internal heat?"
Qíbó said:
"Due to overexertion and fatigue,
the form-*qì* declines,
the *gǔ qì* (grain *qì*) is insufficient,
the upper *jiāo* does not circulate,
the lower *wǎn* does not pass through,
the stomach *qì* is hot,
the hot *qì* smolders in the chest,
therefore internal heat occurs."
The Emperor asked:
"How does *yáng* exuberance generate external heat?"
Qíbó said:
"If the upper *jiāo* is not clear and flowing,
then the skin becomes dense, the pores are closed and obstructed,
the *xuán fǔ* (mysterious openings) are not open,
the *wèi qì* cannot be discharged,
therefore external heat occurs."
The Emperor asked:
"How does *yīn* exuberance generate internal cold?"
Qíbó said:
"*Jué qì* flows upward in opposition,
cold *qì* accumulates in the chest and is not discharged,
if it is not discharged, then warm *qì* departs,
cold alone remains,
then the blood congeals and stagnates,
if it congeals, then the vessels do not flow,
The pulse is full, large, and hesitant,
therefore there is cold in the interior.
62.6 The Yellow Emperor said:
When Yin and Yang combine,
blood and Qi combine,
disease patterns are formed.
How should one puncture for this?
Qí Bó replied:
When puncturing for this,
select from the Jing-sui (channel passages),
extract blood from the Ying level,
extract Qi from the Wei level,
consider the body type,
and adjust according to the seasonal variations of abundance, scarcity, height, and depth.
The Yellow Emperor said:
When blood and Qi combine,
disease patterns are formed,
and Yin and Yang are imbalanced,
how should one tonify or drain?
Qí Bó replied:
When draining excess, insert the needle only when the Qi is abundant,
the needle and Qi are inserted together,
to open its door as if sharpening its hinge.
The needle and Qi are extracted together,
without harming the essential Qi,
then the pathogenic Qi is drained downwards,
the outer door is not closed,
to release its disease,
to agitate and enlarge its pathway,
as if clearing its road.
This is called "large writing."
It must be incisive and released,
then the great qi will be subdued.
The Yellow Emperor said:
"How should deficiency be supplemented?"
Qíbó said:
"Hold the needle without moving it
to settle its intention.
Await the exhalation and insert the needle,
when the qi exhales, the needle enters.
The needle empties, the four directions are blocked,
and essence has nowhere to go.
Insert the needle firmly and then quickly withdraw it,
when the qi enters, the needle comes out,
heat cannot return,
block its gate.
Pathogenic qi is dispersed,
and essential qi is preserved.
Move qi, observe the time,
near qi is not lost,
far qi then arrives.
This is called 'pursuing it.'"
62.7 The Yellow Emperor said:
"Master, you speak of deficiency and excess as arising in ten places,
They arise from the Five Zàng,
the Five Zàng and their five vessels.
Now, the twelve meridians
all give rise to illnesses.
But you, Master, only speak of the Five Zàng.
The twelve meridians
all connect to the three hundred and sixty-five joints.
If a joint is diseased,
it will certainly affect the meridian.
The diseases of the meridians
all have conditions of deficiency and excess.
How can they be reconciled?
Qíbó said:
The Five Zàng
are naturally paired with the Six Fǔ as interior and exterior.
The meridians, collaterals, branches, and joints
each give rise to deficiency and excess.
The location of the disease
should be treated accordingly.
If the disease is in the vessel,
regulate it with blood.
If the disease is in the blood,
regulate it with the collaterals.
If the disease is in the Qì,
regulate it with the Wèi (defensive Qi).
If the disease is in the flesh,
regulate it with the spaces between the muscles.
If the disease is in the sinews,
Treat the sinews if the disease is in the sinews.
If the disease is in the bones,
treat the bones.
Use burned needles and coercive pricking below
and together with urgent cases.
If the disease is in the bones,
quench the needle with medicinal ironing.
If the disease is of unknown pain,
Liǎng Qiāo (兩蹻) is the best option.
If the body has pain,
but the nine pulses show no disease,
then use divergent needling.
If the pain is on the left but the right pulse is diseased,
greatly prick it.
Be sure to carefully examine the nine pulses,
and the way of needling is complete.
*Miù Cì Lùn Piān* (繆刺論篇) Chapter Sixty-Three
63.1 Huángdì (黃帝) asked, "I have heard of divergent needling,

Qíbó (歧伯) replied, "When pathogenic factors invade the body,

If they linger and do not leave,
Entering and lodging in the capillary vessels,
remaining and not leaving;
entering and lodging in the meridian vessels,

The Emperor asked:
"I would like to hear about *miù cì*,

Chapter Sixty-Four: On Acupuncture Against the Natural Flow in the Four Seasons
64.1 Excess in *Juéyīn* (厥阴) causes *yīnbì* (阴痹, Yin obstruction);
deficiency causes heat obstruction;
if slippery, it causes *húshàn* (狐疝, fox hernia);
if wind is astringent, it causes accumulated *qì* (气) in the lower abdomen.
Excess in *Shǎoyīn* (少阴) causes skin obstruction;
indistinct and painful (隱軫) deficiency causes lung obstruction;
if slippery, it causes lung wind hernia;
if astringent, it causes accumulated blood in urination.
Excess in *Tàiyīn* (太阴) causes muscle obstruction;
cold damage and deficiency causes spleen obstruction;
if slippery, it causes spleen wind hernia;
if astringent, it causes accumulated fullness in the heart and abdomen that occurs periodically.
Excess in *Yángmíng* (阳明) causes pulse obstruction and periodic heat in the body;
deficiency causes heart obstruction;
if slippery, it causes heart wind hernia;
if astringent, it causes accumulation and frequent fright.
When the Tàiyáng meridian has excess, one will suffer from bone bi (bì) and heaviness of the body.
When deficient, one will suffer from kidney bi (bì).
If the pulse is slippery (huá), one will suffer from kidney wind hernia.
If the pulse is hesitant (sè), one will suffer from accumulation, occasional headache.
When the Shǎoyáng meridian has excess, one will suffer from sinew bi (bì) and fullness in the ribs.
When deficient, one will suffer from liver bi (bì).
If the pulse is slippery (huá), one will suffer from liver wind hernia.
If the pulse is hesitant (sè), one will suffer from accumulation, occasional sinew tension, and eye pain.
64.2 Therefore, the Qi of spring is in the meridians (jīngmài);
the Qi of summer is in the collateral vessels (sūnlùo);
the Qi of long summer is in the muscles;
the Qi of autumn is in the skin;
the Qi of winter is in the bone marrow.
The Emperor (Dì) said:
I wish to hear the reason for this.
Qíbó said:
Spring is when
the Qi of heaven begins to open up,
the Qi of earth begins to vent,
frost melts and ice thaws,
water flows and channels become clear;
therefore, human Qi is in the meridians.
Summer is when
the meridians are full and Qi overflows,
entering the collateral vessels to receive blood,
and the skin becomes replete.
Long summer is when,
all the meridians and collaterals are flourishing,
overflowing inward into the muscles.
In autumn,
the *tiān qì* begins to contract,
the *còu lǐ* close and become blocked,
and the skin becomes stretched and taut.
Winter is a time of covering and storing,
blood and *qì* are within,
residing internally in the bone marrow,
and communicating with the five viscera.
Therefore, pathogenic *qì*
always enters and lodges along with the *qì* and blood of the four seasons.
As for its changes, they are immeasurable,
but it must follow its meridian *qì*.
Avoid the *xié*,
eliminate the *xié*,
then disordered *qì* will not arise.
64.3 The Dì asked:
If one goes against the four seasons, disordered *qì* arises,
what should be done?
Qíbó said:
In spring, puncturing the collaterals causes
the blood and qi to flow outwards,
causing a person to have little qi.
In spring, puncturing the muscles causes
the blood and qi to circulate in reverse,
causing a person to have shortness of breath.
In spring, puncturing the sinews and bones causes
the blood and qi to stagnate internally,
causing a person to have abdominal distension.
In summer, puncturing the meridians causes
the blood and qi to become exhausted,
causing a person to have loosening of the joints (jiě yī).
In summer, puncturing the muscles causes
the blood and qi to retreat inwards,
causing a person to be easily frightened.
In summer, puncturing the sinews and bones causes
the blood and qi to flow upwards in reverse,
causing a person to be easily angered.
In autumn, puncturing the meridians causes
the blood and qi to flow upwards in reverse,
causing a person to be forgetful.
In autumn, puncturing the collaterals causes
the qi not to flow outwards,
causing a person to lie down and not want to move.
In autumn, puncturing the sinews and bones causes
the blood and qi to disperse internally,
causing a person to have chills.
In winter, puncturing the meridians causes
When qi and blood are both depleted,
it causes blurred vision.
Puncturing the luòmài (絡脈, network vessels) in winter
causes internal qi to leak outward,
leading to severe bìzhèng (痺證, impediment/numbness syndrome).
Puncturing muscles in winter
exhausts the yang qi,
causing forgetfulness.
Generally, these are major adverse conditions when puncturing during the four seasons,
which must be followed.
Acting contrary to them will cause chaotic qi to interact and create disease.
Therefore, if one punctures without knowing the seasonal principles,
or where diseases arise,
treating what should be followed as contrary,
the body's upright qi will be internally disordered,
interacting with the essence.
One must carefully examine the nine diagnostic points.
If the upright qi is not disordered,
the essence and qi will not be disturbed.
64.4 The Dì (帝, Yellow Emperor) said:
Good. Puncturing the five zàng (藏, viscera):
If the heart is hit, death occurs in one day,
and its movement is hiccupping.
If the liver is hit, death occurs in five days,
and its movement is speech.
If the lungs are hit, death occurs in three days,
and its movement is coughing.
If the kidney is injured, death will occur in six days,
and its movement will be sneezing and yawning.
If the spleen is injured, death will occur in ten days,
and its movement will be swallowing.
If a person's five viscera are punctured and injured, death is certain.
As for its movement,

Chapter 65: Treatise on Manifestation, Root, Disease Transmission
65. 1 The Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) asked:
"Diseases have manifestation and root,
and acupuncture has opposing and following.
What is the reason for this?"
Qíbó replied:
"In all methods of acupuncture,
one must distinguish between Yin and Yang,
ensure that front and back correspond,
and apply opposing and following methods appropriately.
Manifestation and root can shift."
Therefore, it is said:
"Sometimes the problem lies in the manifestation and you seek it in the manifestation,
sometimes it lies in the root and you seek it in the root,
sometimes it lies in the root and you seek it in the manifestation,
sometimes it lies in the manifestation and you seek it in the root."
Therefore, treatments sometimes succeed by addressing the manifestation,
sometimes succeed by addressing the root,
sometimes succeed by taking an opposing approach,
and sometimes succeed by taking a following approach.
Therefore, understanding acting against (the natural order) and acting in accordance with it,
and practicing correctly require no questioning.
Knowing the *biāo* (manifestation) and *běn* (root),
every action will be appropriate.
Not knowing the *biāo* and *běn*,
this is called reckless action.
65.2 Now, acting against and acting in accordance with the *yīn* and *yáng*,
the *biāo* and *běn* are the way (to understand things).
From the small, one can understand the large;
speaking of one, one can understand the harm of a hundred diseases;
from the few, one can understand the many;
from the shallow, one can understand the broad.
One can speak of one and understand a hundred.
From the shallow, one can understand the deep;
observing the near, one can understand the far.
Speaking of *biāo* and *běn*,
it is easy, but don't miss it.
Treating against the order results in acting against the natural order;
treating in accordance with the order results in acting in accordance with the natural order.
If the disease comes first, then acting against the natural order comes later, treat the *běn*.
If acting against the natural order comes first, then the disease comes later, treat the *běn*.
If cold comes first, then the disease develops later, treat the *běn*.
If the disease comes first, then cold develops later, treat the *běn*.
If heat comes first, then the disease develops later, treat the *běn*.
If heat comes first, then fullness in the chest develops later, treat the *biāo*.
If the disease comes first, then diarrhea comes later, treat the *běn*.
If diarrhea comes first, then other diseases develop later, treat the *běn*.
It is imperative to regulate it;
then treat other diseases.
For those who develop fullness in the middle *zhōng mǎn* after the initial illness, treat the manifestation;
for those who develop vexation of the heart *fán xīn* after the middle fullness, treat the root.
People have guest *qì* and same *qì*.
If the small and large intestines are unfavorable, treat the manifestation;
if the small and large intestines are favorable, treat the root.
If the disease manifests with excess,
treat the root while addressing the manifestation,
first treat the root,
then treat the manifestation.
If the disease manifests with deficiency, address the manifestation while attending to the root,
first treat the manifestation, then treat the root.
Carefully observe the intervals of exacerbation and remission,
and regulate accordingly.
In cases of remission, treat both simultaneously;
in cases of exacerbation, treat separately.
For those who develop illness after initial unfavorable conditions in the small and large intestines, treat the root.
65.3 Regarding the transmission of disease:
In heart disease, first there is heart pain,
and after one day, coughing;
after three days, hypochondriac distending pain;
after five days, obstruction and non-passage,
body pain and heaviness.
If it does not cease after three days,
death occurs at midnight in winter,
and midday in summer.
Lung disease with dyspnea and cough;
after three days, the hypochondria are distended, full, and painful;
after one day, the body feels heavy and aches;
after five days, there is distension;
if it does not cease after ten days,
death. (Occurs) at sunset in winter,
sunrise in summer.
Liver disease with dizziness and hypochondrial distension and fullness;
after three days, the body feels heavy and aches;
after five days, there is distension;
after three days, there is pain in the lower abdomen and lower back, with soreness in the lower leg;
if it does not cease after three days,
death. (Occurs) at sunset in winter,
early meal in summer.
Spleen disease with body ache and heaviness;
after one day, there is distension;
after two days, there is pain in the lower abdomen and lower back, with soreness in the lower leg;
after three days, there is pain in the back, *jia*, and muscles, with urinary retention;
if it does not cease after ten days,
death. (Occurs) when people are settled down for the night in winter,
late meal in summer.
Kidney disease with pain in the lower abdomen and lower back, and soreness in the *huí*;
after three days, there is pain in the back, *jia*, and muscles, with urinary retention;
after three days, there is abdominal distension;
after three days, there is pain in both hypochondria;
if it does not cease after three days,
death. (Occurs) at great dawn in winter,
late afternoon in summer.
Stomach illness with distention;
in five days, lower abdomen, lumbar spine, and backache become sore;
in three days, back sinews ache and urination is blocked;
in five days, the body feels heavy;
if it does not cease in six days,
death will occur after midnight in winter,
and at midday in summer.
Bladder illness with blocked urination;
in five days, lower abdomen becomes distended, lumbar spine, and backache become sore;
in one day, abdominal distention occurs;
in one day, the body aches;
if it does not cease in two days,
death will occur at cockcrow in winter
and in the late afternoon in summer.
All illnesses successively transmit in this way;
those that are like this
all have a death date.
Do not puncture.
Stopping at one zàng organ
and extending to three or four zàng organs
is when puncturing is permissible.
Tiānyuán Jì Dàlùn, Chapter Sixty-Six
66.1 The Yellow Emperor asked, saying:
"Heaven has the Five Elements,
governing the five positions to generate cold, heat, dryness, dampness, and wind.
Man has the Five Zàng,
transforming the five qì,
To be born with joy, anger, thought, worry, and fear,
you speak of the five movements succeeding each other and all governing them.
At the end of the year,
they cycle and begin again.
I already understand this.
I wish to hear how they correspond to the phenomena of the three *yīn* and three *yáng*.
How do they align?
Guǐ Yúqū bowed his head, prostrated twice, and replied:
"Profound is your question!
The *wǔ yùn* (five movements) and *yīn yáng* are
the Way of Heaven and Earth,
the guiding principles of all things,
the parents of change and transformation,
the fundamental origin of life and death,
the dwelling place of spirit and clarity.
How can one not understand them?
Thus, the generation of things is called transformation (*huà*),
the extreme of things is called change (*biàn*),
the unfathomable *yīn yáng* is called spirit (*shén*),
the unbounded use of spirit is called sagacity (*shèng*).
The use of change and transformation,
in Heaven, is *xuán* (mystery),
in humans, is the Dao,
on Earth, is transformation (*huà*).
Transformation produces the five flavors,
the Dao produces wisdom,
*Xuán* produces spirit.
Spirit in Heaven is wind,
On earth, it is wood;
in the sky, it is heat.
On earth, it is fire;
in the sky, it is dampness.
On earth, it is earth;
in the sky, it is dryness.
On earth, it is metal;
in the sky, it is cold.
On earth, it is water;
therefore, in the sky, it is *qì*.
On earth, it takes form.
Form and *qì* interact and transform, giving birth to all things.
Now, Heaven and Earth
are the top and bottom of all things;
left and right
are the pathways of *yīn* and *yáng*.
Water and fire
are the signs of *yīn* and *yáng*;
metal and wood
are the beginning and end of creation.
*Qì* has much and little;
form has flourishing and decline.
Above and below call to each other,
and increase and decrease become evident.
66.2 The Emperor said:
"I wish to hear how the five *yùn* govern the seasons."
Guǐ Yúqū said:
The five *qì* cycle,
each completing its period on time,
is not solely governing the seasons.
The Emperor said:
"Please tell me what you mean."
Guǐ Yúqū said:
"Your servant has compiled 《Kǎo Tàishǐ Tiānyuán Cè》, which says:
The great void is vast and empty,
initiating the basis of transformation,
and giving rise to all things.
The five *yùn* complete the sky's cycle,
spreading *qì* and true essence,
governing the totality of *kūnyuán* (earthly origin),
the nine stars hang bright,
the seven luminaries revolve,
called *yīn* and called *yáng*,
called soft and called hard,
the hidden and visible are in their positions,
cold and heat relax and stretch,
begetting and transforming,
all things are clearly manifested."
Your servant has studied this for ten generations,
this is what it means.
The Emperor said:
"Good. What does it mean that *qì* has more or less,
and form has waxing and waning?"
Guǐ Yúqū said:
"*Yīn* and *yáng* *qì* each have more or less,
Thus, it is said that there are three *yīn* and three *yáng*.
Forms have waxing and waning;
this refers to the governance of the Five Elements,
each having excesses and deficiencies.
Therefore, in its beginning,
an excess goes forth and a deficiency follows it;
a deficiency goes forth and an excess accompanies it.
Knowing what to welcome and knowing what to follow,
one can predict the timing of the *qì*.
Corresponding to Heaven is called the Heavenly Symbol (*Tiānfú*);
receiving the year is called the Yearly Controller (*Suìzhí*);
the combination of the three is called governance.
The Emperor (*Dì*) said:
How do the upper and lower call upon each other?
*Guǐ Yúqū* said:
Cold, heat, dryness, dampness, wind, and fire
are the *yīn* and *yáng* of Heaven,
and the three *yīn* and three *yáng* serve them from above.
Wood, fire, earth, metal, water, and fire
are the *yīn* and *yáng* of Earth,
and they correspond from below with growth, development, transformation, and storage.
Heaven uses *yáng* to give birth and *yīn* to nurture growth;
Earth uses *yáng* to kill and *yīn* to store.
Heaven has *yīn* and *yáng*,
and Earth also has *yīn* and *yáng*.
Wood, fire, earth, metal, water, and fire
are the *yīn* and *yáng* of Earth,
[governing] growth, development, transformation, and storage.
Therefore, within yang there is yin,
and within yin there is yang.
Thus, if one wants to understand the yin and yang of Heaven and Earth,
the qi of Heaven corresponds with movement and never ceases,
therefore it shifts to the right every five years.
The qi of Earth corresponds with stillness and holding its position,
therefore it returns and converges every six cycles.
Movement and stillness summon each other,
above and below approach each other,
yin and yang intermingle,
and from this, change is born.
66.3 The Yellow Emperor said:
The cycles of above and below,
are they governed by numbers?
Guǐ Yúqū said:
Heaven uses six as its divisions,
Earth uses five as its regulations.
The cycle of Heavenly qi,
six cycles constitutes one full completion.
The completion of earthly reckoning,
five years constitutes one full cycle.
Sovereign fire is used to illuminate,
minister fire is used to position.
Five and six combine to make seven hundred and twenty qi,
which constitutes one j纪 (period).
Altogether thirty years,
one thousand four hundred and forty qi,
Generally, sixty years,
constitute one cycle.
Neither falling short nor exceeding,
all of this is evident.
Dì (帝) said:
"Master's words
above encompass the heavenly cycles,
below exhaust the earthly principles,
truly they can be called complete.
I wish to hear them and treasure them,
above to govern the people,
below to cultivate oneself,
to make the common people understand clearly,
superiors and inferiors in harmony and affection,
virtue and beneficence flowing downwards,
descendants without worries,
to pass on to later generations,
without end.
May I be permitted to hear them?"
Guǐ Yúqū (鬼臾區) said:
"The mechanisms of ultimate numbers,
are subtle and intricate.
Their coming can be seen,
their passing can be traced.
Those who respect them prosper,
those who neglect them perish.
To act against the Dao and pursue selfish interests,
will surely incur heavenly calamity.
I respectfully follow the way of Heaven,
and ask you to speak of essential truths.
The Emperor said:
"Those who speak well of beginnings
will surely meet at the end;
those who speak well of what is near
will surely know what is far.
If this is the case, then the ultimate numbers are exhausted and the Way is not confused,
this is what is meant by being enlightened.
I hope that you, Master, can extend and arrange them in order,
so that they are organized and logical, simple
and inexhaustible,
lasting and unbroken,
easy to use and hard to forget,
and become the framework,
the essentials of the ultimate numbers.
I wish to hear them all."
Guǐ Yúqū said:
"How brilliant is your question!
How clear is your understanding of the Way!
It is like a drum responding to the drumstick,
an echo responding to a sound.
I have heard that,
in years of *jiǎ* and *jǐ*,
the Earth element governs.
In years of *yǐ* and *gēng*,
the Metal element governs.
In years of *bǐng* and *xīn*,
The water (element) governs it.
In years ending in ding (丁) and ren (壬),
the wood (element) governs it.
In years ending in wu (戊) and gui (癸),
the fire (element) governs it.
The Yellow Emperor said:
"How do these correspond to the Three Yin and Three Yang?"
How should they be combined?
Guǐ Yúqū said:
"In years ending in zi (子) and wu (午),
the Shao Yin is seen above.
In years ending in chǒu (丑) and wèi (未),
the Tai Yin is seen above.
In years ending in yín (寅) and shēn (申),
the Shao Yang is seen above.
In years ending in mǎo (卯) and yǒu (酉),
the Yang Ming is seen above.
In years ending in chén (辰) and xū (戌),
the Tai Yang is seen above.
In years ending in sì (巳) and hài (亥),
the Jue Yin is seen above.
Shao Yin
is what is called the "manifestation" (biāo 標).
Jue Yin
is what is called the "end" (zhōng 終).
Above Jue Yin,
wind qi governs it.
Above Shao Yin,
Hot qi governs it.
Above Tàiyīn (太陰),
damp qi governs it.
Above Shǎoyáng (少陽),
minister fire governs it.
Above Yángmíng (陽明),
dry qi governs it.
Above Tàiyáng (太陽),
cold qi governs it.
This is what is meant by the origin.
This is called the Six Elements.
The Emperor said:
How radiant is the Dao,
how clear is the discourse!
I request that it be written on jade tablets
and stored in golden boxes,
and titled "Celestial Element Records."
Chapter Sixty-Seven: Great Treatise on the Five Circulations
67.1 The Yellow Emperor sat in the Bright Hall,
began to rectify the Celestial Net,
oversaw the eight limits,
examined and established the Five Constants.
He invited the Celestial Teacher and asked him, saying:
"The discourse states that the movement and stillness of Heaven and Earth
are governed by the spirits,
and the ascent and descent of yin and yang
manifest signs of cold and heat.
I heard about the numbers of the Five Phases from Fūzǐ.
What Fūzǐ spoke of
was simply that the Five Qì each govern a year.
Starting with Jiǎ (甲) to determine the phase,
I then discussed it.
Guǐ Yúqū said:
"Earth governs Jiǎ (甲) and Jǐ (己);
Metal governs Yǐ (乙) and Gēng (庚);
Water governs Bǐng (丙) and Xīn (辛);
Wood governs Dīng (丁) and Rén (壬);
Fire governs Wù (戊) and Guǐ (癸).
Above Zǐ (子) and Wǔ (午),
Shǎoyīn governs it.
Above Chǒu (丑) and Wèi (未),
Tàiyīn governs it.
Above Yín (寅) and Shēn (申),
Shǎoyáng governs it.
Above Mǎo (卯) and Yǒu (酉),
Yángmíng governs it.
Above Chén (辰) and Xū (戌),
Tàiyáng governs it.
Above Sì (巳) and Hài (亥),
Juéyīn governs it.
They do not align with Yin and Yang,
what is the reason for this?"
Qíbó said:
"This is illuminating the Dao;

The numbers that can be counted

As for Yin and Yang,
they can be counted to ten,
extrapolated to a hundred,
counted to a thousand,

The Yin and Yang of Heaven and Earth

67.2 The Dì (Emperor) said:

Qí Bó said:
"An illuminating question indeed!
I have perused the text of the *Tàishǐ Tiānyuán Cè* (Grand Beginning Celestial Origin Book).
The Qi of Dāntiān passes through the *Niú Nǚ* and *Wù* divisions;

As for what is called the *Wù Jǐ* division,

The origin of observation,

67.3 The Emperor said:

When seeing Yangming,

The Emperor said:

"When Jueyin is on top, then Shaoyang is below,
Zuǒ yángmíng yòu tàiyīn.
When Shǎoyīn is above, Yángmíng is below;
left is Tàiyáng, right is Shǎoyáng.
When Tàiyīn is above, Tàiyáng is below;
left is Juéyīn, right is Yángmíng.
When Shǎoyáng is above, Juéyīn is below;
left is Shǎoyīn, right is Tàiyáng.
When Yángmíng is above, Shǎoyīn is below;
left is Tàiyīn, right is Juéyīn.
When Tàiyáng is above, Tàiyīn is below;
left is Shǎoyáng, right is Shǎoyīn.
The so-called facing south and assigning their positions,
refers to their visibility.
Above and below meet,
cold and heat are adjacent,
if the Qi is compatible, it is harmonious,
if it is incompatible, it results in illness.
The Emperor said:
When the Qi is compatible, why does illness occur?
What is the reason?
Qíbó said:
Because the lower encroaches upon the upper,
which is not in its proper position.
The Emperor said:

Qíbó said:
The upper moves to the right,
the lower moves to the left,
they circle the heavens left and right, having a surplus, and then meet again.
The Emperor said:
I heard Guǐ Yǔqū say:
What corresponds to the earth is still.
Now, you, Master, say the lower moves to the left,

I would like to hear how this comes about."
Qíbó said:
"Heaven and earth move and are still,
the Five Elements shift and return.
Even Guǐ Yúqū only observes these things from above,
and still cannot fully explain them.
The function of change
is that heaven displays its phenomena,
earth completes its form,
the Seven Luminaries weave through the void,
and the Five Elements adorn the earth.
The earth
is that which bears and generates the forms of things.
The void
is that which arranges and corresponds to the essence and qi of heaven.
The movement of form and essence
is like the roots and branches of a tree.
Observing its phenomena from above,
even what is distant can be known."
67.4 The Yellow Emperor said:
"Is the earth truly below?"
Is that not so?
Qíbó said:
The earth is that which is below man,
[and is] within the Great Void.
The Emperor said:
What supports it?
Qíbó said:
The great qi raises it up.
Dryness dries it,
heat steams it,
wind moves it,
dampness moistens it,
cold hardens it,
fire warms it.
Therefore, wind and cold are below,
dryness and heat are above,
damp qi is in the middle,
and fire travels through the spaces in between.
Cold and heat, the six influences, enter,
thus causing emptiness and the arising of transformation.
Therefore, when dryness prevails, the earth is dry;
when heat prevails, the earth is hot;
when wind prevails, the earth moves;
when dampness prevails, the earth is muddy;
when cold prevails, the earth cracks;
when fire prevails, the earth is solidified.
67.5.1 The Emperor said:
As for the qi of Heaven and Earth,
how is it observed?
Qíbó said:
The actions of overcoming and restoration
of the qi of Heaven and Earth
do not manifest in diagnosis.
The *Pulse Method* says:
The transformations of Heaven and Earth
cannot be diagnosed through the pulse.
This is what it means.
The Emperor said:
What about the *jiàn* qi (intervening qi)?
Qíbó said:
It follows where the qi is located,
with its timing on the left and right.
The Emperor said:
How is this timing determined?
Qíbó said:
Following its qi leads to harmony;
opposing its qi leads to illness.
Not being in the correct position causes illness.
Alternately shifting its position causes illness.
Losing its position is dangerous.
When *cùn* and *chǐ* are reversed, it means death.
When yin and yang interchange, it means death.
First establish the year
to know its qi;
corresponding responses should be seen on the left and right;
Then one can speak of the conformity or opposition of life and death.
